articles.title: [In This Economy] The nothing burger that is the Maharlika Investment Fund
articles.summary: While Maharlika is earning money, its reliance on short-term placements and investments in established businesses leaves the promised additional development benefits unclear

blocks.text: At least some Filipinos must be wondering: whatever happened to the Maharlika Investment Fund, which is being managed by the Maharlika Investment Corporation (MIC)?

Well, we know for a fact that the three-year term of MIC’s first president, Rafael “Joel” Consing Jr., is nearly up. It’s been reported that Finance Undersecretary Ma. Angela “Angel” Ignacio is being considered to succeed Consing. The possible change has been linked to supposed dissatisfaction with the fund’s performance (aside from Consing’s reported health issues).

Recall that when President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed the fund into law on July 18, 2023, then-finance secretary Benjamin Diokno called it a “game-changing measure.” We were promised faster infrastructure development, more foreign investment, and high-quality jobs. But how much of that promise has materialized?

According to MIC’s unaudited financial disclosure for the first half of 2026, cumulative deployed capital had reached P24.7 billion by June 30. That’s only about a third of the P75 billion originally contributed by the Land Bank of the Philippines and the Development Bank of the Philippines.
MIC still held P53 billion in cash and cash equivalents, down from P71.1 billion at end-2025. In addition, another P50 billion subscribed by the national government remained unreleased.

The largest recent investment was a P15-billion short-term loan to Petron to finance fuel imports and operating needs, against the backdrop of the US–Iran war and the global oil shock this year. MIC says the loan supports fuel security and carries prevailing interest rates.

That could be useful during an energy crisis, but exactly what financing gap required Maharlika’s involvement? Petron already has other funding arrangements, as the MIC itself acknowledges. The public deserves evidence of the additional fuel supplies or other benefits enabled by this particular loan.

Before this, MIC also acquired additional shares of port operator Asian Terminals in the first half of 2026. Buying shares from existing owners gives Maharlika a claim on future profits. The transaction itself doesn’t finance the construction of new ports, however, and any subsequent improvements in capacity or logistics need to be demonstrated separately.

Meanwhile, MIC exited its short-term financing of Makilala Mining on June 5 by transferring the loan to Equinaire Holdings. MIC reported a 12.5% net annualized return in dollars or approximately 25% in pesos. That deserves credit, although the annualized figures should not be mistaken for the percentage earned over the actual holding period.

Then there’s the much-publicized grid deal announced in January 2025. The proposed major investment through Synergy Grid and Development Philippines, which holds an indirect interest in the National Grid Corporation of the Philippines, remained delayed.
Other initiatives are still underway. A July agreement with the Philippine National Oil Company, for instance, covers exploring a petroleum storage project in Bataan targeted for 2028.

blocks.caption: How much does the Philippines need to build a strategic petroleum reserve?

blocks.text: To its credit, Maharlika seems somewhat profitable. MIC reported P1.24 billion in net income for the first half of 2026 and separately announced a P1.376-billion dividend remittance to the national government in June.

But if you dive deeper, you’ll see that the income comes from mainly cash and short-term placements that generated P1.14 billion in interest. Funds awaiting investment were placed primarily with government financial institutions.
In short, a large amount of money taken from state banks is just earning interest through placements primarily with state financial institutions.

Sure, this preserves liquidity or the ability to access money quickly — at least while deals are evaluated. But earning deposit interest hardly strengthens the rational of why we had to have Maharlika in the first place. It’s not exactly the promised game-changer.

Also, the headline P2.09 billion in portfolio returns includes P1.446 billion in unrealized gains, or increases in investment values that have not been realized through a sale. That’s roughly 69% of the total. Those gains can easily reverse when prices fall.

Running the institution also costs money, of course: operating expenses reached P170.8 million in the first half of 2026, including P111.8 million for professional services. Those costs need to be justified by returns and public benefits beyond what existing institutions could deliver.
Did you know that the president and CEO of MIC earns a salary of P2.5 million per month? Is it worth it, given MIC’s performance? And exactly how much are the other officials and directors earning?

Of course, investment institutions take time to build. Pressuring managers to spend faster could produce worse or overly risky deals, and the unreleased government contribution reflects funding processes beyond MIC’s sole control.

But this brings us to Maharlika’s original problems. Recall that it didn’t create an extra P75 billion of national wealth or “surplus.” What it did, instead, was merely transfer resources from existing public institutions into a new investment vehicle. Those resources have alternative uses, including supporting the state banks’ development lending.

The value of the best forgone alternative is what economists like me call “opportunity cost.” Maharlika’s returns must be assessed against that opportunity cost, with allowance for the risks taken and the expense of running the fund.

Back in June 2023, 21 faculty members of the University of the Philippines School of Economics, myself included, published “Maharlika Investment Fund: Still beyond repair.” We questioned the fund’s unclear rationale, its competing financial and development objectives, and whether it could attract enough additional investment to justify the resources committed to it.

More than three years later, our concerns seem to be borne out. While Maharlika is earning money, its reliance on short-term placements and investments in established businesses leaves the promised additional development benefits unclear.

Likewise, the government must show what additional development Maharlika enables. How much private capital joined projects because of its involvement? Which investments would otherwise have lacked financing? What measurable improvements have reached consumers and communities?

At the very least, Congress should require a public accounting of each investment’s cost, realized earnings, risks, and development results. Large acquisitions and loans should also come with a clear explanation of why existing banks or government agencies couldn’t achieve the same objectives more effectively.

In conclusion, more than three years on, the Maharlika Investment Fund has turned out to be a nothing burger. I’m afraid that an upcoming change in leadership won’t resolve many of its fundamental problems. But as the current administration winds down, expect President Marcos to harp on its purported successes anyway. – Rappler.com

Jan Carlo “JC” Punongbayan, PhD, is an associate professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics. His professional experience includes the Securities and Exchange Commission, the World Bank Office in Manila, the Far Eastern University Public Policy Center, and the National Economic and Development Authority. JC writes a weekly economics column for Rappler. He is also co-founder of UsapangEcon.com and co-host of Usapang Econ Podcast.

His first book, False Nostalgia: The Marcos “Golden Age” Myths and How to Debunk Them, was published by Ateneo de Manila University Press in February 2023. items: Chinese hackers, identified as 'TA419' by Proofpoint, have been impersonating US AI experts to steal emails and passwords from individuals in think tanks, universities, and defense contractors since 2025.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

WASHINGTON, USA – Chinese hackers have been impersonating US AI experts, including a former government official, to try to steal emails from experts in AI at think tanks, universities, and other organizations, the cybersecurity company Proofpoint said on Thursday, October 1.

In a report, Proofpoint said that it had watched the hackers — which it dubs “TA419” — regularly try to steal passwords from people working for US or Japanese think tanks, defense contractors, universities, and law firms since as far back as 2025.

Proofpoint attributed the hacking efforts to the Chinese group based on the types of malware the group used, the internet infrastructure used to carry out the attacks, and the targets it observed the group focusing on, which align with Chinese intelligence collection priorities.

Proofpoint said the hackers’ recent campaign involved writing emails purporting to come from experts in AI or statecraft, including Lynne Parker, who previously worked as the principal deputy director of the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy. Proofpoint said the emails would typically propose AI-themed collaborations or initiatives before steering targets toward password-stealing websites.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately return a message seeking comment. Beijing has long denied carrying out cyberespionage operations.
Proofpoint declined to name the hackers’ targets, saying only that the latter included “experts working on AI regulation, export controls and national AI strategy.”
Reuters was independently able to identify one of them: Alex Engler, a former White House official who now heads the Penn Center on Media, Technology, and Democracy.

Engler told Reuters on Wednesday he had received an email appearing to come from Parker inviting him “to join a new AI policy project.” But he said the email “felt slightly, nebulously off” and, after he checked with others in the field, he realized he was dealing with an impostor.

Engler said he could not speculate about why someone would try to hack him, but Proofpoint said that its view of the targeting — which involved fewer than 10 individuals working for a handful of organizations — suggested “an intelligence interest in US policymaking rather than technology theft alone.”

Parker told Reuters that Engler was one of two people that she knew of who had received suspicious messages purporting to come from her in early July. She added that the allegation of Chinese involvement made sense.

“The United States and China are in a competition around AI,” Parker said. “Trying to get people in the AI policy space to reveal information about their AI policy plans — if that indeed was what the objective was — it’s not surprising.” – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Britain’s nursing union has cut its ties with an Israeli drug company over the firm’s links to the country’s military and track record of corporate misconduct.
The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) has axed Teva UK as a commercial partner and as sponsor of a forthcoming event on migraine and headaches at the union’s London headquarters.

Pro-Palestine groups who were pushing the RCN to drop Teva UK claimed the decision was “a major breakthrough for grassroots healthcare organising and the international boycott, divestment and sanctions movement” aimed at isolating Israel worldwide.
The RCN represents more than 500,000 nurses in the UK. Teva UK is the British arm of the global drug giant Teva Pharmaceuticals, which is one of the NHS’s biggest suppliers of medicines.
It acted after coming under pressure from campaign groups Nurses for Palestine and UK Healthcare Petitions to Royal Colleges (UKHPRC) to end its relationship with Teva UK.
Carmel O’Boyle, the chair of the RCN’s ruling council, confirmed the decision in a letter to Nurses for Palestine.

“Going forward [the] RCN is ending its commercial partnership with Teva UK. Teva UK will no longer be a sponsor of the RCNi nursing leadership summit: migraine and headache services event on 30 October 2026. The event will go ahead as planned,” she said.

“We are taking this action because further due diligence showed that there are a number of Teva Pharmaceuticals’ operations, which have been the subject of legal sanction and public scrutiny, which are not in line with RCNi [the union’s publishing and education arm] and RCN values.
“We know how important it is that the RCN only enters commercial relationships with companies that represent the values of the nursing profession.”
Teva said it was “disappointed” at the RCN’s decision and that healthcare had been “politicised”.
Nurses for Palestine welcomed the move. “Teva has no place sponsoring professional bodies dedicated to healing, care and preserving human life,” a spokesperson said.

UKHPRC said: “It is unthinkable that in this day and age healthcare organisations continue to enter into commercial relationships with companies linked to sustaining state systems accused or found by international bodies to involve grave violations of international law, including crimes against humanity, apartheid and genocide.”
Pro-Palestine campaigners are now calling on the Royal College of Pharmacy to drop Teva UK as a sponsor of its annual conference next month and cancel the exhibition stand the firm has booked.
Teva has been ordered to pay about £1bn in fines and other payments by the European Commission and US authorities over the last decade for bribery, price-fixing and abuse of its market position.

In 2024 the European Commission fined Teva €462.6m for blocking rival firms from competing with Copaxone, its treatment for multiple sclerosis, in seven European countries for between four and nine years.
In 2023 it agreed with the US Department of Justice to pay $225m in fines as an alternative to prosecution after it was charged with fixing the price of three drugs.

And in 2016 it struck a deal with the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the US Department of Justice to pay $519m to settle civil and criminal charges involving its bribery of government officials in Russia, Ukraine and Mexico.

A Teva spokesperson said: “As one of the largest suppliers of medicines to the UK we have valued our longstanding partership with the RCN and the opportunity it has provided to support healthcare professionals and the patients they care for.

“We are disappointed by the RCN’s decision to end this relationship and are seeking further dialogue with the organisation. Healthcare is at its best when it remains focused on patients rather than being politicised.”

articles.title: Almost half of Fayed abuse accusers are potential trafficking victims, MPs told
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Met police say 70 women’s accounts have hallmarks of trafficking, suggesting case numbers could rise

Almost half of the women who reported allegations of sexual abuse by

blocks.text: Almost half of the women who reported allegations of sexual abuse by Mohamed Al Fayed to the Metropolitan police are potential victims of human trafficking, MPs have been told.

In a briefing for the all-party parliamentary group (APPG) for the survivors of Fayed and Harrods in July, senior Met officers said a review earlier this year found 70 survivors’ accounts bore the hallmarks of trafficking.
Last month the Home Office confirmed that at least five survivors were victims of international and domestic trafficking.
The Met’s figures suggested the number of confirmed cases could climb much higher, said the Liberal Democrat MP Wendy Chamberlain, a co-chair of the APPG.
“I can’t believe that wouldn’t increase,” said Chamberlain, who also compared the scale of Fayed’s abuse to Jimmy Savile’s.
The Labour MP Dave Robertson, the APPG’s other co-chair, said: “The number of women who were trafficked by Mohammed Fayed and his trafficking ring is certainly much higher.”

Some women were trafficked from Harrods to Fayed’s private offices and residence in Park Lane while others were taken out of the UK and abused overseas, senior police officers running the Met’s investigation, Operation Cornpoppy, told the APPG.
But several survivors told the Guardian that the Home Office had not recognised them as victims of trafficking because they now live abroad.

Amy, who lives in Italy, said she was trafficked from Harrods, where she initially worked on the shop floor, and her home to Fayed’s other properties. She said she was transferred to a PA role in his private residence and office at 60 Park Lane in London, where he allegedly sexually abused her, including groping her breasts and forced kissing.
She said Fayed also took her in his private car and helicopter to his estate in Oxted, Surrey, where she was sexually assaulted in a lagoon-style swimming pool located behind a concealed door.

“I would be removed from my home in Hammersmith and then be changed into clothes like Lacoste polo shirts and Bermuda shorts and boat shoes, which I absolutely hated,” said Amy. “That was robbing me of my actual identity. Whoever saw me leave my bedsit would say that’s not her. That’s a strong component of what trafficking is and was very calculating.”

blocks.caption: Amy, then aged 21, during a holiday in Venice while she was working for Fayed. Photograph: supplied
A recent photo of Amy. Photograph: supplied

blocks.text: In a letter sent in June to the then minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Natalie Fleet, Amy raised concerns about the apparent exclusion of survivors living outside the UK from the Home Office assessment of potential trafficking victims, the National Referral Mechanism (NRM).

She received a response from the Home Office in August, which said there was not a requirement that a potential victim be resident in the UK before being referred to the NRM by the police, or another first responder organisation.
But last month Amy was informed by her contact officer at the Met that the Home Office had confirmed it would reject any referrals made for international residents.

blocks.caption: Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods (pictured) and other places owned by Fayed. Photograph: Mina Kim/Reuters

blocks.text: KP Law (KPL), which represents Amy and 277 other alleged survivors of Fayed’s abuse, said nearly a quarter of those women now lived overseas.
Lucy Traynor, a senior associate at KPL, criticised the apparently inconsistent advice as to who was eligible to be recognised as a victim of trafficking.

The lawyer said: “We are still seeing individuals whose experiences meet the threshold for trafficking struggling to secure recognition through these systems which are designed to identify and protect victims. Amy’s case is a stark example. Despite the nature of what she experienced, she continues to face barriers to recognition outside the UK. That disconnect between what the Home Office has committed to and what survivors experience in practice is simply not acceptable.”
First responders including police forces and some charities can refer someone to the NRM if they suspect they are a victim of human trafficking.

The Home Oﬃce then makes an initial “reasonable grounds” decision if it believes a crime may have occurred before investigating further and making a final “conclusive grounds” decision. So far it has confirmed that five women allegedly abused by Fayed were trafficking victims.
Eleanor Lyons, the independent anti-slavery commissioner, said the Home Office’s statutory guidance explicitly stated that people needed to be in the UK to be referred to the NRM.

Lyons said this was because the process involved getting access to support including a safe house and counselling, which officials believed would be difficult to provide to people who do not live in the UK.

But she called on the Home Office to reconsider the requirement because many affected people she spoke to just wanted to be recognised as trafficking victims, adding that the situation was causing deep distress for alleged survivors of Fayed’s abuse.

“The government should be doing everything it can to make it easier to identify these women and recognise them as potential victims of modern slavery,” Lyons said. “They’re doing directly the opposite right now, which is causing further harm to the survivors.”

Survivors’ groups say more than 500 women have come forward about abuse that allegedly took place at Harrods, Park Lane, Fulham football club, the Ritz hotel in Paris, and other places owned by Fayed. The Met is investigating 165 victims who have contacted the force directly.

A Met police spokesperson said: “We were previously making referrals to the Home Office for victims living in the UK and abroad, but those relating to victims living abroad were being rejected. As a result, we have paused any further such referrals. Should the Home Office position change, we will restart those submissions. Our support to victims continues, regardless of where they live.”

A Home Office spokesperson paid tribute to “the incredible bravery” of survivors of Fayed’s alleged abuse. They added: “We are ensuring modern slavery survivors get the support they need to recover and move on with their lives.”
A Harrods spokesperson said it “supports all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continues to work closely with the Met police on its investigation”.

articles.title: Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave lands on TIME100 Next list
articles.summary: Shoko Kawata's maternity leave drew mixed reactions in Japan, a country struggling to lift birth rates.

blocks.text: Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named one of the 100 most influential rising stars by TIME Magazine.
The recognition comes weeks after the 36-year-old gave birth to her first child on 15 September.
Earlier this year, Kawata, who is mayor of Yawata City in Kyoto prefecture, was plunged into a national debate about whether elected officials should take time off for childbirth.
Her decision to take maternity leave drew a mix of support and backlash across Japan, a country that is struggling to lift birth rates.

Some on social media said having a baby is tough and Kawata is doing her best. Japanese society has failed to design systems with pregnancy in mind, one claimed. Another said Kawata is setting a wonderful example by putting her family first and making it easier for other women to enter politics.

But critics argued that stepping away from public duties is "irresponsible", and that if Kawata wanted to get pregnant "she should have done so before taking office". One said top officials wanting to take extended leave "should resign".
Others insisted salaries should be cut during maternity leave.

In a sit-down interview with the BBC before giving birth, Kawata brushed off the criticisms, proudly declaring she enjoys her job and believes now is the time for her to have a child and start a family.

"If we were to criticise politicians taking maternity leave, it means we are effectively excluding all women in their 20s through 40s - women who are capable of becoming pregnant - from public office," she said.

While Japan provides maternity leave for city workers, there is currently no legal framework for local elected officials. So Kawata worked with her office to create a plan. She transferred her authority to her deputy mayor Shigeto Nose for 16 weeks, while working remotely when she could.

On 15 September, Mayor Kawata announced she gave birth to a baby girl. She posted a photo on X, external, thanking those who had supported her, and doubled down on her goal to advocate for social issues nationwide.
"As I face the countless challenges that lie ahead and learn what it truly means to be a parent, I want to reflect those experiences in real time into the policies I pursue," she wrote.
"I want to confront the many challenges facing parents and children today from that same perspective, as someone living through them myself, and think about how we can find a way forward together."

articles.title: The Sudan connection: Is Ethiopia at risk of a proxy war?
articles.summary: Ethiopia and Sudan are trading accusations over the armed conflicts they face. Can the conflict dynamics in the wider Horn of Africa exacerbate tensions?

image.caption: While most internet connections are down, pictures of tanks in the city of Alamata are in circulationImage: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: Over the past week, three militias from a new alliance, led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), have been fighting the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) in northern Ethiopia.

The heterogeneous alliance that calls itself the "Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival" brings together seven armed domestic groups that oppose Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's federal government.

However, the ENDF has painted a picture of an alliance that extends far beyond Ethiopia's borders: Its commander-in-chief, Field Marshal Birhanu Jula, accused Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt of supporting the TPLF.

Sudan dismissed the allegation as "baseless." Its military government countered with accusations that Ethiopia was supporting the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia that has been fighting Sudan's army for over three years.
Eritrea said Ethiopia was attempting to shift responsibility for its own internal conflicts onto its neighbors. Cairo, meanwhile, issued a flat denial.
A domestic conflict with "external actors"
Viewing developments in northern Ethiopia as a domestic affair is not the full picture, according to experts.

"While it is primarily a domestic conflict, it certainly has a foreign policy dimension due to the many external actors directly or indirectly involved," said Susanne Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation.
Stollreiter told DW that these actors have their own interests in the region — interests that could potentially be advanced by the conflict.
"If this conflict escalates, I would even assume that it could truly lead to a kind of conflagration across the region, given the various conflict dynamics here in the Horn of Africa."
Mirroring alliances between Ethiopia and Sudan
Egypt and Sudan have long harbored grievances against Ethiopia because the source country of the Blue Nile dammed the river just before the border.
Why Ethiopia's mega dam is causing tensions with Egypt

Sudan has been caught up in a brutal civil war since April 2023. Both sides to the conflict — the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF militia — are believed to have ties to partners that are now fighting on opposing sides in Ethiopia.

On one hand there's the Sudanese government and the TPLF, which was largely defeated in the 2020–22 Tigray War in Ethiopia. Many Tigrayan fighters went into exile in Sudan where they organized as "Army 70" and fought alongside the SAF against the RSF.

"They played quite an important role in the Sudan Armed Forces pushing back against the RSF in eastern Sudan and even into Khartoum. And then that relationship continued," said Magnus Taylor, Deputy Project Manager, Horn of Africa at the think tank International Crisis Group (ICG).
"The issue that the federal government of Ethiopia has is that it appears that Sudan is in a kind of alignment or an alliance with one of the strongest opposition groups in the country."
Tigrayan fighters in Sudan and training camp for Sudan militia in Ethiopia

In May, the Sudanese government hosted high-ranking representatives of the TPLF and leaders of other Ethiopian groups that are critical of Abiy. Some of those groups are now part of the new seven-member alliance.
On the other hand, there's the Ethiopia's central government and the former Sudanese special unit, the RSF.

In February, the news agency Reuters reported on a secret training camp for RSF fighters in the Ethiopian border region of Benishangul-Gumuz. According to the report, the United Arab Emirates provided instructors, funding, and logistical support — claims the UAE denied.
The UAE is closely allied with Ethiopia and, despite denials, is considered the RSF's most important backer.

blocks.caption: A Reuters investigation alleged that hundreds of tents in Western Ethiopia's Benishangul-Gumuz region were put up with the purpose of training RSF fightersImage: Vantor/REUTERS

blocks.text: Is Eritrea involved in the latest conflict?

So far, there are no signs of direct involvement by the Sudanese army or the RSF in the conflict in Ethiopia. There is no evidence of Eritrea's role in the latest escalation either. But there's no shortage of wild speculation.
Eritrea fought alongside Abiy's forces in the Tigray War but the leaders of the two countries had had a falling out by the time the Pretoria peace agreement was signed in November 2022.
Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds

Experts have long suggested that Eritrea — despite denials — is now supporting the TPLF. Distrust of Abiy runs deep, given his stated ambitions to secure Ethiopia access to the open sea — by force if necessary, such as by seizing the Eritrean port of Assab on the Red Sea.
ICG analyst Magnus Taylor told DW that Eritrean involvement in the latest fighting is plausible.
"I think the Eritreans have used the TPLF and other opposition groups to deter the perceived risk of Ethiopian aggression, whether that's for access to the port or other reasons," Taylor said.

"Having a large physical presence within Tigray or within Afar even would be, I guess, a justification for the Ethiopians to carry out more extensive military operations on Eritrea. The Eritrean tactic is to deter military action, not to invite it."
Asmara has strengthened relations with Cairo this year, and the United States has just let sanctions against Eritrea expire.
Why can't Ethiopia and Eritrea be friends?
Is there a risk of a wider regional conflict in the Horn of Africa?
The Horn of Africa borders the Gulf region in the north, which has lost stability due to the Iran war. Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels are also disrupting the Bab al-Mandab Strait. .
In Somalia, Al-Shabab is regaining ground, cooperating with the Houthis despite wide ideological differences.

blocks.caption: Djibouti records many refugees from Yemen these days, due to Houthi advancesImage: IOM Djibouti/AFP

blocks.text: "These are important trade routes that are being disputed and fought over and everyone is trying to profit from the unstable situation," Stollreiter, the head of the Ethiopia office of the Germany's Friedrich Ebert Foundation, said.

"In this respect, it is no real coincidence that so many actors are now becoming particularly strong again, also because of the absence of the actors who were otherwise protective powers in the region."
The US in particular, but also the Europeans tied down by Russia's war in Ukraine, have less of an eye on the Horn of Africa than before, Stollreiter said.
Have Gulf powers taken sides in Ethiopia?
The UAE and Saudi Arabia, which are accused of supporting different warring parties in Sudan and Yemen, and have polarized the entire region in recent years, are all the more present.
Why has the UAE escaped scrutiny over its role in Sudan?
However, ICG's Magnus Taylor does not think that the situation in Ethiopia is at risk of escalating into a proxy war between the Gulf powers.
"While the UAE is a strong backer of Addis Ababa, the Saudis are not strongly backing the TPLF or any other opposition group."

Whether from the Arabian Peninsula, Sudan, or Eritrea — one week after the outbreak of war in Ethiopia, there are no clear signs that the internal conflict is becoming internationalized. However, in the unstable Horn of Africa, that risk is particularly high.
The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict

articles.title: Who was Cesar Virata?
articles.summary: Cesar E.A. Virata, the Philippines" longest-serving finance chief and prime minister under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., passed away on Friday, October 2, at the age of 95.
articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 1:48pm
Cesar E.A. Virata, the Philippines’ longest-serving finance chief and prime minister under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., passed away on Friday, October 2, at the age of 95.
Virata served as finance secretary from 1970 to 1978 and finance minister from 1978 to 1986.
He was the Philippines’ prime minister from 1981 to 1986. He also served as the country’s governor at the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.
As a key figure in economic policymaking, Virata was recognized by the Department of Finance (DOF), among other former secretaries, for his leadership during major crises.
He was at the helm of the DOF when Super Typhoon Yoling and the Great Central Luzon Flood struck the country in 1970.
His death was announced by the Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC), where he served as a director since 1995 and as corporate vice chairperson for 26 years.

Virata was also a longtime educator at the University of the Philippines (UP), where he served as dean of the UP College of Business Administration from 1960 to 1967 and is credited with introducing the Master of Business Administration program.

He graduated cum laude from UP with degrees in Mechanical Engineering and Business Administration before earning a Master of Business Administration in Industrial Management from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.

A biography of Virata, “Cesar Virata: Life and Times Through Four Decades of Philippine Economic History,“ was launched in 2014 by economist and educator Gerardo Sicat after 12 years of research and writing.

“He covered all aspects of the tax system – national and local, and also international taxation. His contributions are beyond tax changes. Many of these were in the nature of administrative decisions as well as the infusion of delicate rules and protocols of tax reviews and investigations,” Sicat said in a paper released in 2011.
Virata’s career in government and academe spanned several decades, making him one of the Philippines’ most prominent economic managers of the postwar era. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Friday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfolded
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: When a passenger plane plunges 17,000ft amid claims of terrorism, hijacking and geopolitical intrigue, Guardian journalists have to try and separate fact from fiction in…

blocks.text: Good morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers.

This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more.
This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world.

So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.

Northern Ireland | Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”.
US news | Tennessee’s governor has suspended all executions in the state and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night.
AI | When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.
Europe news | A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’

blocks.caption: Assaf Regavim filmed the first widely circulated video from inside the cabin. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images

blocks.text: International leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury.

Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilot had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal. Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a “terror attack”. Two Israeli security sources later told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.

Saudi investigators detained the co-pilot upon landing and are cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to determine his reasons and potential affiliations. William Christou, a Beirut-based reporter with the Guardian, tells me: “They’re examining whether it’s a terror attack, whether it had any previous planning or prior direction, and if it could be a lone wolf attacker, who was perhaps motivated by anti-Israel hate, but wasn’t necessarily linked to any larger organisation or state.”
‘The story changed moment to moment’

William began drafting his initial report as soon as he woke up to news alerts about a potential hijacking. The Israeli government originally minimised the incident, describing it as a fight between pilots, while another early report suggested the plane had to land because of a fight between Ukrainian and Russian co-pilots.
“I was sifting through so much misinformation,” he says. “The story changed very quickly, and moment to moment.”

Back in the UK, Oliver Holmes was looking at flight trackers. Now based at Guardian HQ, Oliver has reported extensively across the Middle East. What I didn’t know until we spoke is that he once trained as a pilot, which has left him with an enduring interest in aerospace and aviation.

Flight tracking websites have transformed how we report in-air incidents, he tells me. “Before any government has made an announcement, these platforms can tell you something seriously wrong has happened.”

Flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft rapidly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes, just as it reached to the Saudi-Jordanian border. Oliver suggests that investigators will look at whether this sudden and ferocious plunge was why the plane eventually landed with part of its tail missing.

Oliver sent what he could interpret from the tracking data to his international desk editors, who asked him to work on a tick-tock piece – not, for once, a reference to social media, but an old-school print term for an article that sets out the hour-by-hour narrative of an unfolding news story.

“It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening,” says Oliver. Eventually there came a flood of footage purporting to show images from inside the plane – but was it real? Each clip that the Guardian incorporated into our reporting had to be verified, particularly given the potential for AI-generated fakes. (The Guardian’s head of photography Fiona Shields is fascinating here on how we assess AI images.)
‘Netanyahu was trying to present himself as Mr. Security’

But this wasn’t just an aviation disaster. “It was taking place in this hugely sensitive geopolitical situation,” says Oliver. “The plane landed in Saudi Arabia which does not officially have diplomatic relations with Israel.”

The budget airline itself, flydubai, had by now suspended all its flights to and from Israel, but warned against “premature speculation” while multiple governments, and Israeli officials in particular, were doing just that.

This incident has occurred at a moment of extreme instability across the region, with the strait of Hormuz still closed as a result of the US-Israel assault on Iran and the resurgence of conflict in Yemen. It is also weeks ahead of knife-edge Israeli elections, with polls showing Netanyahu’s current coalition unlikely to meet the threshold needed to form a government but no clear path to power for his rivals.

Just days ago, Netanyahu warned Israel faced an unspecified attack risk during the election period – an assertion greeted with cynicism by political opponents. The Israeli military subsequently confirmed they had no specific intelligence of an anticipated attack. “Most people interpreted that as Netanyahu trying to stir up his base by presenting himself as Mr. Security,” says William.

Nevertheless, Netanyahu’s supporters consider him vindicated. On Thursday, William tells me, the Israeli foreign ministry started briefing diplomats that the flydubai incident was an attempt to drive a further wedge between the UAE and Israel, a relationship already strained after leaks suggesting Netanyahu was personally alerted to the 7 October attacks by the UAE president a week before it took place, something the president has denounced as “an absolute lie”.
‘These stories can be incredibly powerful’

It’s a challenging time to report a story like this, says Taz Ali, who led our live blog which covered the incident unfolding in real-time on Wednesday. “Readers are making connections with what’s happening in the Middle East in general, and you’re trying to answer their questions, first with very scant detail and later with a deluge of information, much of which is proved to be inaccurate.”

Taz, who has a decade of experience in reporting on global events, knows the human drama of a potential hijacking immediately grabs reader’s attention. “Often those stories can be incredibly powerful, involve emergency landings, and sometimes they end in great tragedies”. And with the recent 25th anniversary of 9/11, the incident had an even deeper resonance. “Especially with the anniversary happening so recently, those memories would have been so raw in people’s minds when they came to this story.”
What else we’ve been enjoying

A woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two rounds of lethal injections in Tennessee. Christa Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in 200 years. Pike, 50, has spent three decades on death row after she was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995. blocks.text: Eleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan has become the youngest ever ‘woman grandmaster’ at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board.

Sivanandan, who lives in Harrow, was taught to play by her father when she was five. Within a year, she was beating him and by eight she had beaten the former British champion Peter Lee. If she reaches a rating of 2,500 in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever outright grandmaster.

She fits her chess career around school, but takes everything in her stride. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework,” she says, “but I should be able to manage”. Her ultimate ambition, she says, is simply to be the best chess player in the world.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
articles.summary: The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian forces battle rebel fighters across northern region.

blocks.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict.

On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security.
Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.
The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters.

It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Addis Ababa accusing Eritrea of supporting an alliance of armed groups fighting the Ethiopian government – an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied.
Ethiopia said it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats who "pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security" and would shut its embassy in Asmara.
In response, Eritrea announced on late Thursday that it was severing diplomatic ties with Ethiopia, describing Addis Ababa's decision as "astounding".
"Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision.
The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.

The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people died during that two-year conflict.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of helping the alliance.
A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray also told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines. The BBC has not independently verified the allegation.
But in a rare interview with the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected the accusations.
He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia.
The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.

But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea. Asmara accuses Ethiopia of pursuing what it describes as an increasingly hostile policy over the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.

Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports.
The latest diplomatic confrontation came hours after loud explosions were heard on Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, close to the headquarters of the intelligence service.

A source linked to the opposition alliance told Reuters news agency that its forces had carried out drone attacks in the capital. Ethiopian authorities have not confirmed what caused the explosions, and there have been no official reports of casualties or significant damage.

Residents in two areas of Addis Ababa separately told the BBC that they heard powerful explosions during the night. One resident near the intelligence headquarters said the blast was loud enough to trigger car alarms.

The explosions came hours after Ethiopia's National Intelligence and Security Service imposed an indefinite ban on drone flights over Addis Ababa and surrounding areas, citing the need to protect senior officials, important infrastructure and public events.
Meanwhile, fighting continues across northern Ethiopia.

Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting.

The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there.

Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray.
Independent verification remains difficult because journalists have limited access to the conflict areas and communications across much of Tigray have been disrupted.

The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region.

The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements.
The UN has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: Trillanes: I am not welcome at Senate impeachment court
articles.summary: Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV said Friday the impeachment court should be asked why a subpoena was not issued for him to testify for the prosecution in the impeachment trial of Vice President…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 1:29pm

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV said Friday the impeachment court should be asked why a subpoena was not issued for him to testify for the prosecution in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
In a press conference, Trillanes said he was ready with his testimony.

"Nag-request ang prosecution ng mga isu-subpoena, my name was there last week. Bumalik 'yung mga subpoena ako lang ang wala. Meron bang power na ganyan ang iimpeachment court? May power ba ang presiding officer? They don't have that power kasi diskarte ng prosecution ito. Do not second guess kung ano ba ang itetestify niyan, pakinggan mo muna," he said.

(The prosecution requested for the subpoenas, I was included there last week. But when the subpeona returned, he was the only one left out. Does the impeachment court has that power. Does the presiding officer has that power? They don't have that power because it is a strategy of the prosecution. Do not second guess what will be testified, they should listen first.)
He added the issuance of a subpoena is ministerial.

"Again, bakit hindi mo inisyuhan ng subpoena si Trillanes? Kung ordinary witness ako, hindi niya ako kilala, 'di ba dapat, ano ba, sasabihin n'yo, o sige, gusto nung prosecution, eh di sige. Bakit hindi niya ini-issue? Huwag na tayo umikot pa," Trillanes said.

(Why was a subpoena not issued to me. If I am an ordinary witness whom they do not know, they would say the prosecution wants him to testify so okay, we will issue the subpoena. Why was the subpoena not issued?)

"Sa akin kasi the signal is clear, hindi ako welcome. And by the way, hindi ito collective na parang sinasabi kasi ayaw daw ako ng mga senador. Inisa-isa natin 'yung mga naabutan natin doon. Hindi naman sila nakonsulta kaya next time na may magsabi na kasi may mga ano yung mga senador, don't swallow it right away,” he added.

(For me, the signal is clear, I was not welcome, but this is not a collective sentiment. There were comments that senators do not like me. I asked my former colleagues, and they said they weren’t consulted. So next time someone says senators don’t like me, don’t swallow it right away.)
Trillanes then said that journalists could ask the senator-judges one by one to confirm his account.

“Tanungin ninyo, sino, kasi sabi nung iba hindi naman o kaya better yet, isa-isahin ninyo, Sir, ikaw ba'y kumukontra? Isa-isa ninyo. Ngayon makikita ninyo kung sino talaga ang kumukontra, di ba?,” he added.
(You should ask the senators one by one if they are the ones who are against me testifying for the prosecution.)
It can be recalled that Escudero did not issue a subpoena for Trillanes but said that such decision does not prevent the prosecution from presenting him as a voluntary witness.
The House prosecution panel then dropped Trillanes as one of its witnesses.

The prosecution is presenting evidence for Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President alleging unexplained wealth due to alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision. —AOL, GMA News

Cesar Virata/File photo
Cesar E.A. Virata, the Philippines’ longest-serving finance chief and former Prime Minister under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., died on Friday, October 2, at the age of 95.
His death was announced by the Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC), where he served as a director since 1995 and as corporate vice chairperson for 26 years. No further details were given.

Virata served as finance secretary from 1970 to 1978 and finance minister from 1978 to 1986. He was the Philippines’ prime minister from 1981 to 1986. He also served as the country’s governor to the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.

He was also a longtime educator at the University of the Philippines (UP), where he served as dean of the UP College of Business Administration from 1960 to 1967 and is credited with introducing the Master of Business Administration program at the institution. — Jon Viktor D. Cabuenas/RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: UP scientist on Super El Niño: Prepare for heavy rains, too
articles.summary: Heavy rains and storms remain possible even during generally dry El Niño conditions.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A University of the Philippines scientist urged the public to prepare not only for drier conditions expected during a Very Strong El Niño, but also for possible episodes of heavy rain.

Rafaela Jane Delfino of the UP Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology said the public cannot control when El Niño and La Niña occur or how intense they become, but can take steps to reduce their impacts.

"So naturally occurring itong El Niño and La Niña, and essentially parang hindi natin mako-control kung kailan siya bumabalik, kung gaano siya kalakas. Ang kaya lang natin sigurong maikontrol is kung paano natin mababawasan 'yung impact niya," Delfino said in a video from the University of the Philippines on Thursday, October 1.
("El Niño and La Niña are naturally occurring, and essentially, we cannot control when they return or how strong they become. What we can control is how we reduce their impacts.")

PAGASA said a Strong El Niño is already active in the tropical Pacific and is expected to intensify into a Very Strong El Niño between September and December 2026, then persist through the first half of 2027.
Climate Change Commissioner Albert Dela Cruz has described the developing event as potentially the most severe the Philippines may experience on record.
Heavy rains still possible
While El Niño generally increases the likelihood of below-normal rainfall, dry spells, droughts and water supply stress in parts of the Philippines, it does not mean rain and storms will disappear.

PAGASA's September 23 climate advisory said above-normal rainfall may still occur over the western parts of the country due to the southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones even as generally drier conditions prevail elsewhere.
The Climate Change Commission has likewise warned that intense tropical cyclones, including those reaching super typhoon strength, may still occur during El Niño conditions.

"Maaaring umabot sa kategoryang super typhoon ang mga bagyong ito at magdulot ng malawakang pagbaha," the agency warned. ("These cyclones could reach super typhoon strength and cause widespread flooding.")
Warmer Pacific
Delfino explained that El Niño is characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.

Under normal conditions, easterly trade winds push warm surface water toward the western Pacific. During El Niño, these winds weaken, allowing unusually warm water to spread eastward across the tropical Pacific.

For the Philippines, this shift generally favors drier-than-normal conditions. PAGASA likewise defines El Niño as the abnormal warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, accompanied by cooler-than-average waters over the Philippine Sea.
"Kaya inaasahan natin, during El Niño conditions, relatively drier sa Pilipinas," Delfino said. ("That is why we expect relatively drier conditions in the Philippines during El Niño.")
Delfino said scientists monitor sea surface temperature anomalies, among other indicators, to characterize the strength of an El Niño event.
She noted that current anomalies in parts of the monitored Pacific are already more than 2 degrees Celsius above normal, a level associated by some scientists with the informal term "Super El Niño."

"Papunta pa lang tayo sa peak. Developing pa lang siya. So kaya siya tinatawag na Super El Niño kasi literally, off the charts," Delfino said. ("We are still heading toward the peak. It is still developing. That is why it is being called a Super El Niño because it is literally off the charts.")
PAGASA, however, officially uses the classification "Very Strong El Niño" and expects the phenomenon to peak toward the end of 2026.
Preparing for both extremes
Delfino said reducing El Niño's impacts begins with understanding the hazards it may bring and preparing accordingly.
For agriculture, she suggested establishing rainwater harvesting systems, particularly in rain-fed areas, and planting drought-tolerant crops.
Water management preparations could include early planning for dam operations and reducing household water consumption.
But preparations should not focus exclusively on drought.
"Pero huwag din nating kalimutan na kailangan pa rin nating maghanda sa malalakas na ulan," Delfino said. ("But let us not forget that we still need to prepare for heavy rains.")

articles.title: UP Rural High School condemns red-tagging following Martial Law remembrance activity
articles.summary: The University of the Philippines Rural High School (UPRHS) in Los Baños, Laguna has condemned the alleged red-tagging of the school and its constituents on social media following its observance of…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 1:13pm

The University of the Philippines Rural High School (UPRHS) in Los Baños, Laguna has condemned the alleged red-tagging of the school and its constituents on social media following its observance of an institutional activity remembering Martial Law.

In a statement late Thursday evening, UPRHS called out social media posts by Facebook accounts identified as "Emjay Chico" and "Lorraine Baddie" or Lorraine Badoy, former National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC).

The two accounts raised questions about the school activity, which was reported by UPRHS' official student publication, The Ruralite, regarding the University of the Philippines (UP) Day of Remembrance held on September 21.
UPRHS said the annual activity is an institutionalized UP event commemorating the declaration of Martial Law and reflecting on a significant period in Philippine history.
The school said its program was "student-initiated and student-led," properly communicated to parents, and conducted with the necessary permits and institutional approval.
Participation was also voluntary, UPRHS said.
The program included a resource person who discussed the role of the media in addressing historical distortion about Martial Law.
"We categorically reject the use of red-tagging as a means of intimidating, silencing, or casting suspicion upon our students, faculty, and staff," UPRHS said.
The school also rejected insinuations that students were being exploited, saying that keeping learning safe does not mean shielding young people from difficult questions and realities.
"We will continue to nurture students who respect human rights and uphold the fundamental values of truth, justice, and freedom," it said.
As of posting time, The Ruralite disabled comments to its posts on UP Day of Remembrance activities in UPRHS.
In his post, Chico questioned why the high school students were allegedly involved in a political activity inside school premises.
He stressed that while political participation is a right, children must also be protected from exploitation, manipulation, and undue political influence.

"A school should be a safe space for learning, not a venue for using minors to advance political interests. The responsibility of school officials is not merely to facilitate activities, but to protect the welfare, dignity, and rights of every learner," he said.
Badoy reposted Chico's post and said, "UP Rural School in Bay, Laguna HANDS OFF OUR CHILDREN!"
GMA News Online has sought comment from Chico and Badoy but they have yet to provide statements as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Jeus Yape claims PH’s 4th gold in Asian Games with virtual taekwondo triumph
articles.summary: Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape shines in the debuting virtual taekwondo event, securing the Philippines' first-ever Asian Games gold medal in the sport

blocks.text: REPRESENT. Taekwondo athlete Jeus Yape of the Philippines in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games.
Roderick Yape Facebook page
Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape shines in the debuting virtual taekwondo event, securing the Philippines' first-ever Asian Games gold medal in the sport
MANILA, Philippines – Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape delivered the Philippines’ fourth gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games in Japan, after ruling the mixed individual virtual taekwondo on Friday, October 2.
Yape scored a 2-0 win over Vietnam’s Chau Ngoc Tuyet Sang in the final at the Toyohashi Gymnasium as the country won its first-ever taekwondo gold in the continental showpiece.
In virtual taekwondo, which debuted in the Asian Games, competitors wear virtual reality headsets and motion-tracking sensors to control their digital avatars.

Similar to fighting games, athletes have health bars that their opponents must deplete through successful attacks. Virtual taekwondo also incorporates video game elements like a stun meter, which, when filled, leaves an opponent temporarily defenseless.

Yape also beat Saudi Arabia’s Dunya Bushuaib Saber in the round of 16, Japan’s Hayate Suzuki in the quarterfinals, and Kazakhstan’s Rita Bakisheva in the semifinals on the way to becoming the third Filipino athlete to strike gold in this Asian Games after gymnast Carlos Yulo and pole vaulter EJ Obiena.
It is the second Asian Games medal for the 22-year-old Yape, who also won bronze in the men’s individual poomsae the day prior.
With four golds, the Philippines has matched its tally in the 2018 Jakarta-Palembang, Indonesia, and 2023 Hangzhou, China, editions. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Staff fears grow that BBC will shut its Three and Scotland channels next week
articles.summary:
Redundancy process suggests home of Gavin and Stacey and Fleabag could go online-only again in £500m cuts push

The BBC has started a redundancy process in its TV and streaming division,…

blocks.text: The BBC has started a redundancy process in its TV and streaming division, heightening staff fears that Matt Brittin will announce the closure of the poorly performing BBC Three and BBC Scotland channels next week.

The corporation’s director general, who has repeatedly said that linear TV and radio services may have to shut as audiences move online, is expected to inform staff on Wednesday of the latest stage of a plan to save £500m and shed up to 2,000 jobs.

This week, Dan McGolpin, the director of the BBC iPlayer and Channels division, which includes all the corporation’s TV stations, called for expressions of interest across the department in taking voluntary redundancy.

In an email he said the plan to “mitigate the number of [enforced] redundancies” included sounding out staff interest about job-sharing arrangements, a reduction in hours, and “relocating to another BBC base across the UK”.

The move has fuelled speculation that the BBC is about to take the two channels online-only, according to sources, as Brittin focuses on cutting back on TV and radio services and content that delivers the least value for money.
“It is no secret that BBC Scotland and BBC Three are very expensive on a cost-per-viewer basis – a key metric being looked at – and they clearly haven’t achieved what was hoped,” said one insider.

It would be the second time BBC Three has been taken off linear broadcast. The youth-focused channel – which launched in 2003 and generated hits including Gavin and Stacey, Fleabag, Killing Eve and the lockdown hit Normal People – moved online-only in 2016 to save costs.

Since making a comeback to linear TV in 2022, it has struggled as audiences increasingly drift to streaming TV and video platforms such as YouTube. BBC Three recently announced it was canning the high-profile RuPaul’s Drag Race UK owing to financial pressures.

blocks.caption: RuPaul’s Drag Race UK was recently cancelled owing to financial pressures. Photograph: BBC

blocks.text: On Tuesday, the channel’s highest-rating show was Stacey Dooley Sleeps Over, which was broadcast in a primetime 9pm slot but only managed an average audience of 74,000.

Typically about 4% of the UK population watch the channel live in a week. Its cost per user hour was 26p in 2023-24 and 18p in 2024-25, the last year the BBC broke out statistics for individual services. This compares with 10p for BBC One that year, 9p for BBC Two and 6p for BBC Four.
BBC Three’s budget was doubled to about £80m when it returned to linear TV, rising to £90m in 2023-24, but it was cut to £66m in 2024-25.
A similar online-only fate is looming for the BBC Scotland television channel, which was launched in 2019 as a dedicated outlet for Scottish programming, separate to the Gaelic-language BBC Alba.

According to the BBC’s latest annual report to 31 March just 12% of people in Scotland watch the channel live. That compares with 54% of the adult population consuming BBC Scotland content each week across BBC TV/iPlayer, BBC Radio and BBC Online.
The BBC Scotland TV channel had a budget of £42m in 2024-25, while its cost per user hour was 13p.

“If most of an audience is getting things on demand, we have to look at the value and the cost of all of those different services,” Brittin told BBC One’s Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg programme. “When’s the right time to migrate that service fully to being on-demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer.”

In June, the BBC announced plans to cut 60 jobs in Scotland, to save £10m. The BBC Scotland channel has received about £250m in funding since its launch but has failed to attract large audiences. Its flagship news magazine programme, The Nine, was scrapped two years ago after some episodes drew as few as 1,700 viewers.

blocks.caption: BBC Scotland is watched live by 12% of the Scottish population. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: One source believes that completely shutting the TV channel would be too politically difficult for the BBC, and that an online-only future would be a cost-effective and acceptable solution.
Brittin has also suggested radio services could be axed, having already announced that between 350 and 400 hours of audio content will be cut by the end of the next financial year.

The corporation has already made a number of cost-saving announcements, including permanently reducing the presenter roster on Radio 4’s Today after the departure of Amol Rajan. It also axed the evening news programme The World Tonight after more than 50 years.

In 2010, Mark Thompson, then director general, proposed shutting the Asian Network and 6 Music. Ultimately both survived following a backlash, although the Asian Network was relocated to Birmingham last year and had its dedicated news bulletins replaced by Newsbeat two years ago.
Cost per user hour, the Asian Network, Radio 1Xtra and Radio 3 are the most expensive of the BBC’s stations.
The BBC said it did not comment on speculation.

articles.summary: The dictator’s longtime finance chief and one of his top technocrats, Cesar Virata had deep ties to the Ferdinand E. Marcos regime even as he sometimes pushed back against Imelda Marcos and powerful…

blocks.text: FORMER PRIME MINISTER. Cesar Virata speaks before the congregation at the 122nd proclamation anniversary of the Iglesia Filipina Independiente, also known as the Aglipayan Church, at the National Cathedral of the Holy Child in Manila on August 3, 2024.
Angie de Silva/Rappler

The dictator’s longtime finance chief and one of his top technocrats, Cesar Virata had deep ties to the Ferdinand E. Marcos regime even as he sometimes pushed back against Imelda Marcos and powerful cronies over project spending and economic policy

items: Cesar Virata, a key economic technocrat during the Marcos dictatorship, passed away at the age of 95.
Virata's legacy is complicated by his association with the Marcos regime, which was marked by crony capitalism and economic challenges.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Former prime minister and longtime finance chief Cesar Virata died on Friday, October 2. He was 95.

Virata was one of the Philippines’ most prominent economic technocrats and a central figure in economic policymaking during the Marcos dictatorship. He served as secretary and later minister of finance from 1970 until the fall of Ferdinand E. Marcos in 1986, making him one of the longest-serving finance chiefs in Philippine history.

He was also prime minister from 1981 to 1986 and held senior positions in economic planning, the Board of Investments, Monetary Board, Land Bank of the Philippines, and Philippine National Bank. He represented the Philippines at the World Bank and Asian Development Bank, and chaired the joint World Bank-International Monetary Fund (IMF) Development Committee from 1976 to 1980.

Virata became a part of the circle of economists and administrators who provided the Marcos regime with technocratic expertise during Martial Law. Scholars have described him as the regime’s “chief technocrat,” with strong links to the IMF, World Bank, business community, and academe.

His reputation for technical competence, however, also contends with the dark legacy of the Marcos dictatorship. His economic team operated inside an authoritarian government marked by unabashed crony capitalism and corruption. During his tenure as finance chief, the Philippines also accumulated heavy foreign debt and eventually plunged into a severe economic crisis in the early 1980s.

Virata’s technocrats at times clashed with Imelda Marcos and politically connected businessmen over spending and economic policy. Virata opposed several of the then-first lady’s projects and attempts to tap government funds, including a 1982 request for $12 million in government funding for a film festival in Manila. (READ: [ANALYSIS] Correcting misleading claims by ex-president Marcos’ technocrats)

He also challenged the coconut levy and monopolies associated with Marcos allies Danding Cojuangco and Roberto Benedicto. But his technocratic group could not consistently overcome figures who enjoyed direct access to Marcos and had their own economic power base.

Before his entrance into the world of Malacañang, Virata had built a career in the classroom. A mechanical engineering and business graduate of the University of the Philippines who later earned a master’s degree in business administration from Wharton, he became a professor and served as dean of the UP College of Business Administration from 1960 to 1967.

UP eventually renamed the college the Cesar E.A. Virata School of Business in his honor, a decision sustained by the Board of Regents in 2014 after debate within the university partly due to his extensive service under the Marcos regime.

Rizal Commercial Banking Corporation confirmed Virata’s death in a disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange on Friday. Virata had served as an RCBC director since 1995 and had been the bank’s corporate vice chairperson for 26 years. – Rappler.com
