articles.title: Swing-and-a-miss: MLB rescinds idea to host baseball game in national park after backlash
articles.summary:
Officials in Wyoming had called notion to host game in Grand Teton national park ‘deeply unwelcome’

Major League Baseball (MLB) leadership…

blocks.text: Major League Baseball (MLB) leadership is no longer considering holding a game inside a national park, according to a letter commissioner Robert Manfred sent to officials in Teton county, Wyoming, on Thursday in what could be the league’s biggest swing-and-a-miss off the diamond.

On 26 September, the Washington Post reported that MLB had reached out to the White House about staging a one-day game at Grand Teton national park in Wyoming. Teton county describes itself as a “a year-round resort community” and sits within the Jackson Hole valley. It’s also a habitat for grizzly bears, osprey, bison and more.

News of MLB’s outreach to the federal government quickly sparked concern about the impact that erecting a field and the infrastructure to hold spectators could have on the natural landscape and habitat of scores of wildlife that call the 310,000-acre (125,500-hectare) park home.

In the letter, Manfred noted that MLB had held games at places like the Fort Bragg military base in North Carolina and the nation’s oldest Negro Leagues stadium in Birmingham, Alabama. He added that MLB staff had been doing their due diligence to see whether a game at Grand Teton was possible and to evaluate the potential environmental impact.
“Since the story was reported, it has become clear that the local community does not want us to continue Grand Teton national park as a potential site,” Manfred wrote.
The outrage over the possible MLB game comes as national parks across the US struggle under funding cuts, staffing shortages and consistent overcrowding.
after newsletter promotion
A Teton county commissioner, Luther Propst, who described the potential game as an “incomprehensible and deeply unwelcome notion”, celebrated the MLB’s decision in a post on Facebook.

“Ever since I got a call from the Washington Post about [MLB] scouting a ballfield in Grand Teton National Park, I have been hoping this idea would die a quick death – and today it did!” he wrote. “This is what can happen when we stand up firmly together, and I am proud to have played my part.”

In a statement to the Guardian, a White House spokesperson said that it was approached by the MLB about the possibility of hosting the game but the National Park Service had not granted any permits to do so and the game is not a White House directive.
Neither MLB nor the National Park Service immediately responded to the Guardian’s request for comment.

articles.title: OpenAI fires workers for mishandling 'sensitive information'
articles.summary: The former employees were investigated for sharing data with an outside AI evaluation group.

blocks.text: OpenAI has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling information, including work that involved an external organisation that analyses artificial intelligence (AI) models.

"Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work," a spokesperson told the BBC.
The ChatGPT-maker did not name the sacked workers, but at least two of them were involved in safety research at the firm.
The firings come as the debate over AI safety and the risks the technology may pose to humanity has intensified in recent weeks.
"We have parted ways with three individuals for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information," OpenAI's spokesperson said.
The BBC understands the former employees were not let go for raising safety concerns but for allegedly mishandling sensitive information.
Concerns over AI safety have made headlines after some researchers and industry executives called for more guardrails around the technology.
OpenAI has come under under intense scrutiny after its models went rogue and hacked several platforms, including Australian government websites.
In an earlier incident an OpenAI system accessed the internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face.
That incident led OpenAI to conduct a broad review of the activities of its AI models - called agents, which are designed to execute tasks autonomously based on simple instructions.
The AI lab said this week that it has notified more than 100 organisations about incidents involving unauthoritised activity linked to its AI systems.
Being notified "does not mean that any private information was accessed" or that a system was compromised, OpenAI said.

articles.title: Labor targets ‘visa hopping’ international students in crackdown on ‘permanently temporary’ migration
articles.summary:
Migration agents and lawyers ‘selling false hope’ to people seeking to stay in Australia also in government’s sights as it seeks to reduce overseas arrivals

“Visa hopping” international…

blocks.text: “Visa hopping” international students, migration agents and lawyers trying to “game” the migration system will be targeted by the government, as Labor unveils a further crackdown.

The changes announced on Friday mean international students will soon need to apply for a separate visa to transfer courses, on top of previously announced rules that prevent transferring to a lower grade course, such as switching from a bachelor or masters’ degree to a vocational program.
In a speech to the Migration Institute of Australia, the assistant minister for international education, Julian Hill, said the changes will stop the increase of “permanently temporary” migration.

“When Australians go to another country they do not believe they have some God-given right to hop around from visa to visa for years or decades and game other nations’ appeals and courts systems – and neither should guests in our country,” Hill said.

In a social media post, the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said: “As of today there are new rules to put an end to student visa hopping. It’s all about ensuring we have a migration system that Australians can be confident in.”

The changes are part of a broader reform package to lower net overseas migration, but the government has been forced to amend rules without separate legislation, because it does not have the support of the Coalition or the Greens.
Labor wants to bring net overseas migration down from its current annual level of almost 300,000 to 225,000 by 2028.

Separately, there are now more than 400,000 people on bridging visas, a temporary visa that can be issued if a visa expires and the person waiting for a decision on their next application, or for asylum seekers or non-citizens. A large cohort of these can be international students applying for a different visa – the government is trying to bring this number down.

Hill said from 1 July 2027, a student’s visa will not be extended even if they are transferring into a different course, to prevent “rorting and ensures students can’t just not turn up for the first 6 months, fail their subjects then go to a cheaper provider”.
In the interim, a student won’t be able to transfer within 12 months of beginning a course.
Migration agents and lawyers selling “false hope” by helping individuals to pursue baseless visa claims to help them stay in Australia longer will also be targeted under new rules.
The government is proposing changes to ban migration agents assisting with an application “they know, or reasonably ought to know, does not have a reasonable factual or legal basis”.
Hill said the department of home affairs will consult on how to ensure migration lawyers are also held to account for similar poor practices.

“Increasingly sophisticated forms of migration-related misconduct and a small number of bad actors cause disproportionate harm, often targeting people at vulnerable points in their lives when they are highly susceptible to misleading claims, false promises and unrealistic assurances,” Hill said.
“Taking cash in those circumstances is not helping people – it’s exploiting them and selling false hope.”

Hill said one lawyer specifically submitted an application with the intention of it being refused, it could then go to the administrative appeals tribunal and be refused again and then ultimately be submitted for a ministerial intervention.

“We have also seen some pretty outrageous online advertising by lawyers. Ads that appear to coach people on how to claim they’re bisexual when they’re not, or how to convince the Department they’re being persecuted when they’re not, in order to support a protection claim,” he said.
“The current system for lawyers authorises and arguably requires them to act for clients in ways that damage the administration of and public confidence in Australia’s migration system.”

articles.title: Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell
articles.summary:
New York attorney general brought in by governor after recent questions raised over university’s 2024 investigation

Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said Thursday she is appointing…

blocks.text: Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, said Thursday she is appointing Letitia James, the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang-rape at Cornell University.

“The young woman at the center of this case deserves to know that every fact will be examined and justice pursued,” Hochul said in a statement. “This action will ensure that the matter is fully and thoroughly investigated without conflict or bias, and handled independently with the rigor that this matter demands.”

In her statement, Hochul said the decision by Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county ⁠district attorney, not to prosecute the 2024 case, and the questions raised in recent days over the Cornell police department’s investigation of the allegations, have “undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the district attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time”.
Hochul said James would oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury.

The former Cornell University student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024 filed a lawsuit in September, in a case that has sparked national outrage, roiled the Ivy League campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.

Van Houten declined at the time of the alleged assault to bring any criminal charges, but this week said he would reopen the investigation based on new information in the woman’s lawsuit, which identifies her only by the pseudonym Jane Doe.

He has maintained that the woman’s first account to police didn’t include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. After CBS News this week revealed details from the police interview transcript, he told the network he’d never seen her detailed account and had relied instead on a statement written by a campus police officer and signed by the accuser.
She is suing seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, as well as the university, the fraternity and others.
Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they perpetrated a sexual assault. One said his client hadn’t touched the woman or engaged in any drug use.
Cornell has said it suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely and disciplined or expelled some students, but the university has declined to provide specifics, citing student privacy rules.

Under pressure from the public and politicians, including Hochul , the private university agreed Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.

articles.title: EU ministers mull new ways to curb irregular migration
articles.summary: The proposals include setting up so-called return hubs outside the EU and strengthening the border agency Frontex. Greece has even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency…

image.caption: The EU wants to implement tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns [FILE: April 5, 2019]Image: picture-alliance/NurPhoto/N. Economou

blocks.text: The interior ministers of European Union countries met in Luxembourg on Thursday to discuss ways to strengthen border controls and curb undocumented migration into the 27-member bloc.
Following the talks, they approved a new regulation to boost deportations of irregular migrants.
It will allow member states ​to establish so-called return hubs outside the EU for migrants who are legally required to leave the bloc but cannot be returned to their countries of origin.
Countries including Denmark, Austria, Greece, Germany and the Netherlands have been exploring options to change migration policy and set up such migrant centers.
How the far right hardened Europe's migration stance
What did the ministers say?
"When it comes to return hubs," Danish Interior Minister Morten Bodskov told reporters, "it's progressing very well."
"We are moving in the right direction," he said without providing further details.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said there were "preliminary" talks on return hubs but declined to say which countries were involved.
More work was needed to make sure any agreement would withstand possible lawsuits, he said.
"These agreements are meant to be sustainable in the long term," Dobrindt noted, adding that he was nevertheless hopeful that a first deal could be sealed by the end of the year.
Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink said a technical mission already visited a potential host country in early September.
Supporters of the policy say return hubs could facilitate repatriations and act as a deterrent for would-be irregular migrants.
But critics question their legality and argue that they violate migrants' fundamental rights.
Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing
Suspending asylum process in emergencies?
On Thursday, Greece even proposed temporarily suspending asylum applications in emergency situations. The right to seek asylum is guaranteed by the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
Athens argued that current rules are inadequate to handle mass arrivals as in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.

The Spanish government estimates over 72,000 migrants entered Ceuta in late July. While most of them have since returned, some 10,000 remain, reinforcing calls in some EU capitals for a tougher approach. The Spanish government has said only minors and small groups of the people who entered Ceuta were brought to mainland Spain.
Greece's proposal appeared to draw support from some member states.

"We have to find a legal way not to bring them into the asylum procedure," said Dutch Migration Minister van den Brink. "In situations like Ceuta, it should be treated as ​a border management issue rather than an asylum issue."

Asked whether he saw a suspension of asylum as possible under the new emergency law, ​Magnus Brunner, EU commissioner for migration, said: "Europe needs the means to protect its borders at all times," while stressing that "we will always comply with fundamental rights and values."
How the EU compromised its values on migration
Plans to curtail irregular migration
The interior ministers' talks come as undocumented migration remains high on the EU's political agenda, with far-right parties increasingly gaining support across the bloc.
The situation has pushed many governments towards tougher migration policies centered on border controls, deterrence and returns.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this month that the Commission will propose an emergency tool for countries to better deal with mass migration movements.
But details are still being worked out.
There are also plans to strengthen the EU's border agency, Frontex, with many stressing the need for the organization to have a rapid intervention force that could intervene in border crises.

articles.title: SpaceX flight led by first Black female commander sets US speed record
articles.summary:
Four astronauts pulled up at International Space Station after eight-hour express flight led by Jessica Watkins

Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after…

blocks.text: Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a US speed record, and that created further history with the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit.

SpaceX launched commander Jessica Watkins and her crew for Nasa after a three-week delay to fix their Dragon capsule’s leaking fuel system. Thick clouds threatened all morning to halt the countdown but in the end, the skies cleared enough to allow for a safe liftoff.

With the late-morning launch from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Watkins became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. A geologist who worked with Nasa’s Mars rover Curiosity a decade ago, Watkins is making her second trip to the space station following a lengthy stay in 2022.
“Thanks for an amazing ride,” Watkins radioed following liftoff.

Although their stay at the ISS will last a long six months, the flight there was the quickest yet not only for Elon Musk’s company, but any American entity, including Nasa. The space station’s convenient location when the astronauts launched enabled the fast transit.

blocks.caption: From left, Joshua Kutryk, Luke Delaney, Jessica Watkins and Sergey Teteryatnikov at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on Thursday. Photograph: Jennifer Briggs/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The fresh arrivals include a Canadian man whose wife will give birth while he’s away.

Aside from Watkins, the other astronauts are newcomers to space: Nasa’s Luke Delaney, a retired marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner. They will replace four astronauts who have been living at the orbiting laboratory since February.

This was the 13th crew launched by SpaceX for Nasa, not counting 2020’s test flight. The Crew-13 designation in their mission patch pays homage to Apollo 13, the harrowing 1970 moonshot that ended with the astronauts’ safe return.

References to the number 13 abounded Thursday. Watkins and her crew rode to the launch pad in black Teslas bearing plates that read “Lucky 13”. They also carried up a small crocheted golden dragon named Lucky with a four-leaf clover around its neck.

“We figured it wouldn’t hurt to bring a little of our own luck just in case, but clearly we don’t need it,” Watkins said from orbit, noting they were “four of the luckiest humans on or off planet Earth”.
Heather Kutryk will give birth while her husband is orbiting Earth, making him the fourth man to become a father while doing so. Heather is due to give birth to their third child in late November.

“A lot of life-changing things can happen over six months,” Nasa manager Dana Weigel said on the eve of liftoff, noting that the space agency would do its best to keep Kutryk looped in to his family.The Canadian Space Agency also promised to support the family.

In 2004, Nasa provided a radio link between space station astronaut Mike Fincke and his wife’s delivery room during the birth of their daughter. Five years later, Randy Bresnik, commander of next year’s Artemis III mission, dialed in to his wife’s hospital from orbit.

The happy news traveled more slowly for Austrian astronaut Franz Viehböck. His daughter was born a few hours after he launched to the Soviet Union’s Mir space station in 1991. He was not informed until the next day.

Three hours after Crew-13 blasted off, SpaceX launched a Falcon rocket from California with more than 100 mini satellites. Another Falcon was set to soar late Thursday night from Florida, with a classified satellite for the national reconnaissance office. All this comes the same week the company’s massive Starship reached orbit for the first time.

articles.title: Kanye West’s sold-out Russia concerts cancelled, organisers confirm
articles.summary:
Russia’s foreign ministry had called planned shows unacceptable due to rapper’s ‘glorification’ of Adolf Hitler

Two sold-out shows that

blocks.text: Two sold-out shows that Kanye West was due to play in Russia have been cancelled after weeks of confusion, organisers have confirmed.
The US rapper, who now goes by the name Ye, had been due to perform at the Gazprom Arena in St Petersburg on 10 and 11 October.
In a post shared on the messaging app Telegram on Thursday, the organiser Say Agency said the shows would no longer go ahead.
“Friends, it is with sincere regret that we inform you that the Ye concerts in St Petersburg on the scheduled dates will not be able to take place,” the Moscow-based agency wrote.
“In the near future, we will reach out to you with an official statement regarding the status of the project and future plans.

“Say Agency is very grateful to everyone who has been by our side these past month and a half: supporting us, worrying, and, like us, waiting for these concerts with all their hearts. We remain in touch and continue to work.”
The agency added that ticket refunds would be available from Monday 12 October, with details “about the rules and conditions for refunds” to follow.

There have been weeks of confusion over the status of the shows. Gazprom Arena initially posted enthusiastically about the concerts on social media, calling Ye “the most influential musical artist of our time”. Then in August, after the shows sold out, it said it had not signed an agreement to lease the stadium to the concert promoters, so the gig could not take place on its site.
The arena stressed that it “was not and is not” responsible for the booking and acknowledged that it had received complaints about the shows.
The Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, previously called the planned shows unacceptable due to Ye’s “glorification” of Hitler.

A politician, Nikolay Novichkov, called for the musician to be investigated for praising Hitler and said the concerts should be cancelled unless he publicly declared “moral support for Russia and the special military operation”.
Last year Ye started selling swastika T-shirts and released a song called Heil Hitler.
In January, he took out a full-page advert in the Wall Street Journal to apologise, titled: “To Those I’ve Hurt.”
He wrote: “I am not a Nazi or an antisemite. I love Jewish people.”
The rapper said his bipolar disorder led him to fall into “a four-month-long, manic episode of psychotic, paranoid and impulsive behaviour that destroyed my life”.

Ye’s plan to play in Russia – following in the footsteps of Paul Oakenfold, DaBaby, Jason Derulo and Akon – flouts sweeping sanctions and calls for culture boycotts after the country invaded Ukraine in 2022.

In April, Ye’s show in France was postponed after he was denied a UK visa, which led to the cancellation of his headline appearances at London’s Wireless festival, amid the backlash after his antisemitic remarks.

Ye had been due to perform at the Pulse of Gaia festival at the RCF Arena in Reggio Emilia in July but the city’s prefect, Salvatore Angieri, stopped the gigs after “concerns” were raised by the local Jewish community.

Despite the controversy, fans have been undeterred from seeing Ye live when concerts have been allowed to proceed. His first major concert in the US for more than five years was held in Los Angeles in April. He has also performed to vast audiences in Turkey, the Netherlands, Georgia, Albania, Portugal and Kazakhstan, with more dates planned for the US and Indonesia. The shows come in support of his 12th solo album, Bully, released in March.
Ye has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Trump threatens to hit Iran 'very hard' if Tehran found to be behind FlyDubai incident
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the copilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be struck "very hard" for the attempt on the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump speaks at an event in Denton, Texas, on Thursday. (Alex Brandon/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the copilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be struck "very hard" for the attempt on the lives of more than 180 people aboard the jet.
Investigators still working to determine cause after co-pilot stabbed captain

U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that if Iran is linked to the co-pilot who tried to crash an Israel-bound flight, the Islamic Republic would be hit "very hard" over the attempt on the lives of more than 180 people aboard the jet.

Trump issued the warning as investigators worked to determine why the co-pilot stabbed the flight's captain, causing the FlyDubai plane to plummet before others on board stopped the attack and landed the airliner in Saudi Arabia.
The president was asked by reporters at the White House whether he had been briefed about any links between the co-pilot behind the attack and Tehran.
"We're working on it right now," Trump said. "I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes, but we're working on it right now."
Trump did not elaborate about why he suspects Iran might be involved.
India celebrates pilot who averted disaster on FlyDubai plane
Asked if the U.S. would retaliate against Tehran if it was behind the attack, Trump said, "Oh they'll be hit, very hard, don't worry."
"You just ask them," he said. "They know what happened. They'll be hit very hard."
Stalled diplomacy
His remarks came as diplomatic efforts to end the war appear to have stalled.

Iranian officials indicated Wednesday that they had received an official U.S. response to Tehran's latest proposal to end the seven-month war, which Trump had publicly rejected just days earlier. The officials did not say what the response contained and whether it was a rejection.

items: Trump rejects Iranian proposal to open Strait of Hormuz and end fighting

blocks.text: Trump said in a Time magazine interview published Thursday that he would not accept proposals from Iran that "he wouldn't have approved a year ago," and left open the possibility of resuming bombing after the Nov. 3 U.S. election.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military has dispatched roughly 9,000 troops aboard a group of ships to the Middle East, a U.S. official said Thursday. That could mean three aircraft carriers will be in the region as soon as late October, according to the official, who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.

Despite Trump's public rebuff, mediators have continued working with Iran and the U.S. to try to broker a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz, according to officials who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

articles.title: Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
articles.summary: A voter mobilisation campaign has registered huge numbers of young people but it is not clear who they are backing.

blocks.text: Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.

The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.

"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."

Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.

"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.

More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.

He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.

"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.

He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.

I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.

"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.

"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."

"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.

"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.

"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."

He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."

Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.

The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.

"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."

Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

articles.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
articles.summary: Amid global tumult, the two countries alliance is not the only unlikely pairing.

blocks.text: Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping €1bn (£850m) a day.

Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.
That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.

"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.

"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."

Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.
"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."

According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".
"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.
The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around €1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.
Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.
According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.
That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.
"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.
But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.
However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.

"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.
But there's also the question of security.

On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.
This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a €12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.
MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.

"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.
Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.
Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.
In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.
Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.

No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.

Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank.

"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).

"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me.
In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality".

Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me.

In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere.

In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles.

There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected".
He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else.
With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times.
But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis.

He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want.

That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers.

Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles.

However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities.
Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.
Top image credit: PA / Nur Photo via Getty images

articles.title: What's gone wrong at Nike? How the world's sportswear giant lost its mojo
articles.summary: Several self-inflicted mistakes have cost the biggest sportswear brand on the planet in recent years.

blocks.text: It's been a difficult few years for Nike.
The largest sportswear brand on the planet, named after the ancient Greek goddess of victory, has been losing of late. Losing sales, losing customers and losing ground to its rivals.
The one-time industry disruptor is now the establishment and in the middle of a tricky turnaround plan aimed at clinging on to market dominance.

Nike's latest financial results show signs a turnaround strategy put in place by company veteran Elliott Hill, who was coaxed out of retirement two years ago to lead the firm, is working - but the pace of change is more marathon than sprint.
However, its recovery has been dented by the loss of football star Kylian Mbappé, who ended his 20-year association with the brand last week to join fast-growing Swiss rival, On.
The Real Madrid striker's departure raises the question of whether Nike can remain the top logo for not just elite athletes, but also the fans that idolise them.

To be clear, Nike is still a mega brand and popular the world over. But missteps have seen hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value as its share price tumbled by 75% over five years.
Last month, Nike was ejected from the S&P 100 stock market index of the biggest blue-chip firms in the US.
So what's gone wrong? And can Hill turn things around?

Matt Powell, a veteran analyst and adviser in the sports retail industry, reckons Nike has made "several strategic errors" which have been difficult to reverse, including cutting ties with retailers to sell only direct to customers online and making limited editions items more available.
"The more broadly available those shoes became, the fewer people were interested," Powell says.
Other self-inflicted wounds he suggests include spending research and development cash on digital operations rather than new products.
"They really shut down their innovation on product. Someone jokingly said they were trying to turn Nike into eBay."
The gamble - spending its entire basketball budget on Jordan before he had even competed in the NBA - made Nike what it is today.
The company built a shoe brand around him - Air Jordan. The red and black colours broke NBA rules, but Nike used it as a marketing stunt and paid the fines.
In years that followed Nike partnered with generational talents Tiger Woods, Serena Williams and Cristiano Ronaldo, who all donned the Swoosh on their way to golf, tennis and football greatness.
While the brand retains partnerships with long-retired Jordan, plus Williams and Ronaldo - Woods ended his association in 2024.

"[I'm] not saying that what they did wasn't great, but it was in the past," said Tim Derdenger, an academic in marketing and strategy. "It's not the future and it's not the current and that is what drives apparel sales today."
Nike's books still boast top athletes, ranging from Rory McIlory to Vinicius Junior.
However, it has now lost its biggest footballing star in Mbappé, who had been with Nike since he was nine years old, along with World Cup winner Lamine Yamal.
Yamal suggested his move to Adidas gave him the chance to stand out from Nike's star-studded roster, while Mbappé said On would see him "surrounded by innovators who dream of the same things I do".
Was that a parting dig at Nike?
For all the "doom and gloom", Nike will stay number one, according to Powell - millions worldwide, including young people, remain loyal - but its mistakes have dented its dominance.
"Will Nike be the gorilla they once were? I don't think so. Can the brand come back to growth and profitability? Yes," Powell says.
"When you shut down innovation, you don't turn it back on and it goes right back to full speed," he adds.
Powell thinks Nike's turnaround plan, called "Sport Offense", will start to show positive signs next year.
Hill said Nike had "more work to do" on its sportswear, Jordan brand and in China as the company announced quarterly revenues of $11bn (£8.3bn), which undershot analysts' expectations.
Notably, the company cited "headwinds" in China, where revenue declined by 26%.

articles.title: Enter Shikari announce indefinite hiatus from 2027: ‘We don’t think we’re splitting up’
articles.summary:
Rock band will still tour the UK, Europe and US over the next year but say decision to ‘fall dormant’ feels ‘liberating’

The British rock band Enter Shikari have announced they will go on…

blocks.text: The British rock band Enter Shikari have announced they will go on hiatus at the end of 2027, a decision that may result in the band’s “extinction”.
The St Albans band, who formed in 1999 as Hybryd, are due to tour the UK in November, Europe and the US next year, and said they hoped to play some of their favourite places “one last time”.

A statement from band reads: “As of December 31, 2027, Enter Shikari will fall dormant as a recording and performing entity. This dormancy may eventually end with an eruption back into activity, or may end with extinction, we have no idea which.

“As everyone keeps reminding us, 2027 will be 20 years since the release of our debut album. We’ve been playing music together since we were 15, and friends longer still, but there’s no doubt this is a huge milestone.

“For the past two decades, we’ve run amok in a cultural landscape that elevates easily-pigeonholed art, so being an Enter Shikari hasn’t always been easy, professionally or personally, with obvious negative impact on one’s mental health when tasked with coming up with the goods.

“But we do this because we love it, and we are lucky enough to have built an audience who understand that the less-trodden path is sometimes the more interesting journey. However, it gets to the point where the often difficult terrain of that path starts to frazzle and drain the humble traveller.

“We are far from being the same kids who recorded that debut album, and as much as we love what we do, and still love being in each other’s company, as humans our priorities and capacities have changed.”
The band said their lead singer, Rou Reynolds, had suffered “recent illness” but they had already had “difficult conversations” about their future before that.

“To then see a friend in trouble made those conversations more pertinent,” the statement reads. “While we don’t think we’re splitting up, we do not have a diary that extends beyond 2027 … Maybe we’ll be like Fugazi and just get together to rehearse for fun, without feeling the need to make anyone else listen to it.
“All we really know is after two decades of being a professional band, not having plans three years in advance is liberating.”
The band also said they were working on new music, which fans “should get to hear sooner rather than later, along with another thing we’ve just finished filming”.
Enter Shikari added that they would not be announcing a “farewell world tour”.
The statement concludes: “It’s not the sort of statement we thought we’d be making if you’d asked us a year ago, but we felt it was time to let you know our headspace.
“We really hope we’ll be seeing you over the next 14 months or so, somehow. But if not, all that remains to be said is thank-you for your support, your sweat, your passion, your energy.”
Since forming in 1999, the band have released six UK top 10 albums, including a No 1 with A Kiss for the Whole World in 2023.
They have also scored a handful of hit singles including Anything Can Happen in the Next Half, Juggernauts and Sssnakepit.

articles.title: Joshua Kutryk's launch to the ISS is another example of the important role Canada plays in space exploration
articles.summary: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk blasted off to the International Space Station for a six-month mission just a few months after fellow Canadian Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon. It's an example of…

image.caption: The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft lifts off Thursday morning with Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk on board. (Philip Scott Andrews/Reuters)

blocks.text: Science·Analysis

Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk blasted off to the International Space Station for a six-month mission just a few months after fellow Canadian Jeremy Hansen flew around the moon. It's an example of not only Canada's continuing role in space exploration but also how bright the future could be.
'It's been a big year, a big year for Canada,' says Industry Minister Mélanie Joly
Canadian Joshua Kutryk is in space, on his way to the International Space Station (ISS) after a flawless launch from Cape Canaveral, Fla.
The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket blasted off at 11:10 a.m., right on time.
He and his crewmates — NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — are slated to dock with the ISS after roughly eight hours in space.

items: Crew-13 astronauts, including Canada's Joshua Kutryk, on their way to dock with ISS

blocks.text: The launch is Kutryk's first, and he felt it.
"I'm in space. I don't really believe it yet. It does feel weird, though," he said. "It's good to be here."
'It does feel weird': Canadian astronaut on entering space

This is a historic moment for Canada. It's the first time two Canadians have launched into space in such a short time. Jeremy Hansen launched as part of NASA's Artemis II mission for a trip around the moon only six months ago.
Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly was at the NASA press site shortly after the launch and noted the important role Canada has played and can play in space.

items: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is in 'high spirits' for Thursday's launch to the International Space Station

blocks.text: "It's been a big year, a big year for Canada," she said.

"And now we look forward to seeing how Josh Kutryk's work will continue to obviously participate in international efforts about space exploration and space co-operation, but also to inspire so many young Canadians and older ones that are very much fascinated by space."
Canada's continuing role
Undoubtedly, there have been tensions between Canada and the U.S., but not when it comes to space.

While it's true that NASA has cancelled Lunar Gateway, which would have included Canadarm3, it wasn't due to any political strain between our two countries. Rather, it was a shift in mission priorities brought forth by NASA administrator Jared Isaacman.

Earlier this year, Isaacman announced that NASA was adding a mission to the Artemis Program, which aims to return humans to the lunar surface by 2028. And that resulted in the cancellation of the lunar space station and a focus on constructing a lunar base.
Asked by the CBC at the post-launch news conference about Canada's collaboration with NASA in its future plans, Isaacman hinted that Canada could play a vital role in the future of a lunar base.
"Canada has immense expertise in robotics, clearly, as demonstrated from the Canadarm performance from shuttle to the ISS," he said.

"As the base becomes operational, it should almost be the last choice to send somebody outside in that very demanding and dangerous environment. And you're going to need extensive robotic capabilities … and we're going to be counting on it as part of the architecture."

items: This medical device heading to space with Joshua Kutryk is also helping people here on Earth

blocks.text: It's not only robotics that Canada is looking to contribute, but also lunar rovers.

In December 2025, the CSA awarded four Canadian organizations with contracts totalling $3.2 million for the development of a lunar utility rover that would be used for science, transportation and more to support astronauts on the lunar surface. (Unfortunately, in March the CSA announced the cancellation of another, smaller rover that would have conducted scientific missions on the moon.)
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk lifts off for 6-month ISS mission

"We want to play a bigger part in everything linked to space exploration, but particularly with the moon," Joly said on Thursday. "Being able to have more of a Canadian presence, particularly on the robotic side."
Part of Isaacman's Artemis program restructuring included the speeding up of launches in the Artemis program.
On Thursday, Joly said Canada is ready.
"We know that NASA wants to go further, faster," she said. "We want to do more of that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Montreal hospital isolates patient exhibiting Ebola symptoms
articles.summary: A Montreal hospital has isolated a female patient presenting with symptoms of Ebola, a deadly virus, officials said.

image.caption: A CHUM spokesperson said all necessary safety measures have been put in place and stressed that there are currently no concerns regarding public exposure. (Hugo Therrien/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
A Montreal hospital has isolated a female patient presenting with symptoms of Ebola, a deadly virus, officials said.
Hospital says there are currently no concerns regarding public exposure
The patient arrived at the Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM) late Thursday afternoon exhibiting signs of the disease.
Irène Marcheterre, a spokesperson for the CHUM, said that as soon as the suspicious symptoms were identified, the hospital immediately enacted its required isolation protocols.
The hospital reiterated that all necessary safety measures have been put in place and stressed that there are currently no concerns regarding public exposure.

articles.title: Trump's trade rep sounds pessimistic about deal with Canada, saying issues are 'quite difficult to resolve'
articles.summary: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but that the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a…

image.caption: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer speaks during the second day of the G20 Trade Ministerial Conference at the Pfister Hotel in Milwaukee on Thursday. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but that the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a resolution any time soon.
Jamieson Greer says while 'technical talks' are ongoing, there are 'a handful of outstanding issues'
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 01, 2026 7:01 PM EDT | Last Updated: 27 minutes ago

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he regularly speaks with his Canadian counterpart, but the two sides have reached an impasse on some trade irritants and there's no sign of a resolution any time soon.

Speaking to reporters at the G20 meeting of trade ministers in Milwaukee, Greer sounded pessimistic about the prospect of a deal with the Canadians saying while "technical talks" are ongoing between trade experts from both countries there are some fundamental disagreements.
"The reality is there are a handful of outstanding issues that are quite difficult to resolve," Greer said.
Greer said the Trump administration's policy of imposing tariffs on foreign manufactured goods to try to "reindustrialize" America is a universal one and not "focused on one country."

items: Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates

blocks.text: Canada, meanwhile, maintains that punishing tariffs on industrial products like steel, aluminum and autos make no sense given just how integrated the two economies are after decades of free trade.

The federal government has strenuously opposed U.S. tariffs designed to decimate those key Canadian sectors, saying it's no way to treat a supposed ally. Plus, Canada is America's biggest customer, purchasing more American-exported goods than any other country.
U.S. losing manufacturing jobs

Still, Greer said Canada and other countries treat the United States as "a dumping ground" for their products and the U.S. just wants to produce more of what it consumes domestically. He added that these policies shouldn't be read as "threats against Canada" alone.

Despite Greer's claims that these tariff policies are boosting industrial employment, data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics compiled by the Economic Policy Institute shows that some some, 62,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since Trump took office for his second term in January 2025.
Carney laughs at Trump's claim that Canada will apologize to U.S.
International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, who is responsible for non-U.S. trade, met with Greer while in Wisconsin.

The conversation was focused primarily on wider world trade issues like ending forced labour and the phenomenon of some countries like China dumping heavily state-subsidized products into market economies.
But the Canada-U.S. dispute did come up, Sidhu said in an interview with CBC News.
He said he stressed to Greer that the two countries need to "find a way to work together, especially for our auto supply workers."
"I think there is energy from both sides," Sidhu said, calling it a "very cordial conversation."
"But we want a good deal," he said. "We won't accept anything less."
Greer downplays Trump's deal comments

Speaking earlier Thursday to Bloomberg News from the summit, Greer seemed to downplay President Donald Trump's assertion this week that the Canadians would come calling for a deal and that something could come together within a month.
"You've heard the president talk about this. Most recently he said, 'Well, we may have a deal with Canada in a few weeks.' I'd emphasize the 'may' in that part of the situation," Greer said.

items: Trump trade adviser says Canada will 'pay even more dearly' if 'you interfere' in U.S. midterms

blocks.text: Greer reiterated that the U.S. is open to a deal with Canada, but he suggested Prime Minister Mark Carney and his negotiators can't accept what the Americans are offering.

"The question is does Canada want to get to 'yes' on some of these things. We have a trade policy where we're not inclined to go to zero tariffs because we're trying to reshore," he said. "Gaps remain between Canada and the United States."

Those "gaps" became apparent when Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, with Carney pulling his negotiators back from Washington after what he described as a series of last-minute American changes that weren't workable for Canada.

Canada was concerned about U.S. tariffs on medium- and heavy-duty trucks, which could have made a GM plant in Oshawa, Ont., that produces Chevrolet Silverados uncompetitive and imperiled the planned production of Ford F-250s in Oakville, Ont.

items: Carney says trade deal became untenable when U.S. 'asked too much and offered too little'
Carney outlines the last-minute changes U.S. tacked onto trade deal terms

blocks.text: Carney also said he couldn't accept language in the proposed deal that could have compromised Canada's sovereignty, namely provisions he described as limiting the government's ability to make trade deals with other countries.
U.S. opposition to Canadian policies designed to promote the "discoverability" of French-language programming on streaming services was also an issue, Carney has said.

While Greer seemingly backed down from U.S. demands on French-language content in an interview with CBC News, no apparent progress has been made on those other issues in the weeks since the bilateral talks imploded.
Carney said this week he thinks it's possible to negotiate a "mutually advantageous trade arrangement" with the U.S. at some point in the future.
"Canada stands ready to negotiate in good faith," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

J.P. Tasker is a journalist in CBC's parliamentary bureau who reports for digital, radio and television. He is also a regular panellist on CBC News Network's Power & Politics. He covers the Conservative Party, Canada-U.S. relations, the Crown in Canada, health policy and the Senate. You can send story ideas and tips to J.P. at jp.tasker@cbc.ca

articles.title: Falling glass and ‘decapitated’ plants: the race to protect Edinburgh botanic garden’s plants
articles.summary:
After five years of work, 5,750 panels of toughened glass will help keep hundred of plants safe from Scottish winters – but more work needs to be done

In the early autumn sunlight, Royal…

blocks.text: In the early autumn sunlight, Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh’s extensive plant collection appears safe in their glass enclosures. But danger lurks from above for the tropical ferns, cycads and rare alpine heathers.

Soon the September sunshine will give way to the storms and gales of the Scottish winter, which can bring hundreds of glass panels crashing to the greenhouse floor on the windiest days. Nobody is allowed inside when the wind is above 30mph.

“We’ve had plants that have essentially been decapitated by falling bits of glass,” says Sadie Barber, the glasshouse curator at RBGE. “You go into one of these tropical spaces in winter and there’s icy air coming in. It’s traumatic for those of us who put decades into caring for these plants. A storm can literally just wipe them out.”

blocks.caption: Prof Julia Knights, regius keeper and CEO of RBGE, officially opening the doors. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: But this week, change is in the air for the creaking infrastructure at the 356-year-old botanic garden, the second oldest in Britain after Oxford. On Friday, the palm houses are reopening after five years of painstaking restoration work, complete with 5,750 panels of toughened glass to keep out the elements.

Before they closed for renovation works, the horticultural team had installed a net in case panels fell from the weathered structure. The new ones are not bulletproof – but they are strong enough to resist a bird strike.

blocks.caption: Damage to one of the glasshouses after a storm. Photograph: Helen Pugh Photography

blocks.text: Part-Georgian, part-Victorian, the £23.5m refurbishment has kept nearly all of the original sandstone and wrought iron shell. Inside, more than 600 temperate plants have returned to the building. The air is clean and crisp, purified by ferns that naturally remove toxins from the air. Its temperature and humidity is still controlled by the original pulleys and winches.

“We have made it one vast cathedral-like space for temperate plants,” says Prof Julia Knights, the garden’s regius Keeper and the royally appointed chief executive. She points out her favourite tree fern, which comes from Tasmania and has a Scottish liverwort growing on its woody stem. “They can grow outside in our botanic garden in Logan on the west coast of Scotland because of the oceanic climate,” she says.

blocks.caption: Extensive work has been done to replace and strengthen panels at the greenhouse. Photograph: Helen Pugh Photography

blocks.text: Founded by two physicians in 1670 to teach doctors about medicinal plants, RBGE has morphed into one of the most important collections of plant biodiversity in the world. Its research glasshouses are stuffed with rare ginger species, bananas, blueberries and dozens of begonias.

It is a global authority on rhododendrons and ferns, houses rare plant species that have gone extinct in the wild, and its scientists have helped pioneer new technology, such as DNA barcoding which is used to identify plant species. Arthur Conan Doyle studied here, infusing Sherlock Holmes novels with his botanical knowledge. Today, conservation is its primary focus.
after newsletter promotion

“Our conservation collections are so important to have. The threats are extreme in the wild,” said Prof Pete Hollingsworth, RBGE’s director of science. “The driver[s] for environmental damage are so strong, so having these ex situ safe sites is really important,” he said.

blocks.caption: New display benches in the restored building. Photograph: RBGE

blocks.text: But the restored palm houses aside, many of the glasshouses used to care for the plants are decades past their originally intended lifespan and are waiting for upgrades. Leaks from Scottish rain rot the rootstock of plants, sometimes killing them. Last year, horticulturalists were not allowed inside the greenhouses for 20 days due to high winds. In 2026, they have been shut out 15 times. When they return, they have often worn hard hats and safety gear to pick out the broken glass.

“The glasshouses are the one thing we don’t want to break. It’s the plants inside that suffer,” said Barber. “I was looking at one of our records the other day of a plant we lost in the lowland tropical house. It just had ‘storm’ written next to it. It had either suffered from the cold, or even been cut by falling glass.”

articles.title: The wealthy Cuban Americans ready and waiting for Havana to fall
articles.summary: Cuban exiles in Florida are increasingly hopeful that regime change in Cuba is now on the horizon.

blocks.text: This influential community of Cuban exiles has detested the Communist-run government ever since the late revolutionary leader Fidel Castro expropriated their lands and nationalised their families' companies after taking power in 1959.
And they have wielded their political and economic clout in Florida over the years to shape Washington's policies towards their homeland.
Sixto fled the island as a teenager. Now a real estate developer in his early 80s, his organisation is drafting plans for what he calls "the day after" in Cuba.
The CANCC has created a proposal for a Cuban Stock Exchange and formed committees on everything from energy infrastructure to food security.
Post-Communist planning is nothing new in Miami.
Countless documents and logistical plans have been drawn up by interest groups over the decades, some of them more sober and measured than others.

The difference now, insists Sixto, is the Trump administration's push to force total change on the island. And he says they have the ear of some high-profile contacts including people close to the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio.
"Together with deliveries of humanitarian aid and medical supplies, we'd go and do business in Cuba right away," says Sixto.
In Cuba itself, such claims are mostly met with scepticism.

In the face of Washington's "maximum pressure" campaign on Cuba, the island's leadership recently announced 176 economic liberalisation measures. The Cuban President, Miguel Díaz-Canel, said they were "to advance the defence of socialism, to support and widen social justice".

To his critics, they look distinctly like full-blown capitalism - lifting the cap on the number of workers in a private business, allowing the direct hiring and firing of Cuban employees and permitting ownership of multiple enterprises at once, including by Cuban Americans.

Still, the attendees at the CANCC meeting dismissed the economic reforms as cosmetic, saying they gave no meaningful guarantees to investors. They would "not put a foot into Cuba", Sixto said, while the current regime remained in place.

Some analysts think such planning meetings are premature. Although Cuban Americans are convinced that change is imminent in Cuba, none can say with any certainty what it will be - a US military operation as seen in Venezuela in January? Or a new economic pact with the island's leadership?

"Right now, the very high expectations created by the US administration that some kind of 'day after' was coming soon, or that Cuba would 'be next' have been kicked down the road," says Mike Bustamante, associate professor of history at the University of Miami.

With the November mid-term elections in the US approaching and the Trump administration embroiled in the "quagmire" of the Iran war, Bustamante argues there is little appetite for further foreign adventures.
"It's really tough to think that they will escalate further than what they're doing which is this drip-drip-drip of sanctions."

With the island's oil supply effectively shut off since January, that is already a significant escalation, says Mike Bustamente. Although they have made life unbearable for most ordinary people, they haven't yet "created the ingredients for a political inflection point" in Cuba, he adds.
The Cuban government has not commented on the CANCC itself. But traditionally such groups prompt indignation among revolutionaries who insist they will not be forced out by their critics in Miami.

I ask some guests if they can appreciate the irony that the same people who support a major source of the island's misery – the decades-long US economic embargo and the current fuel blockade – are now hatching plans for its reconstruction, without the input of most Cubans.

For Cuban-American agricultural expert Hugo Orizondo it is only practical to draw up a road map to Cuban development. "Right now, Cuba is like a black hole, we don't know what is happening over there," he admits. "But we do know the potential [for investment]."

Orizondo says he understands the reticence among Cubans to see foreign investors buying up something as sensitive as the rights to arable land. "But what are they going to do with it?" he retorts. "When investors come, they bring money and technology into the land."
Both are urgently needed, he says, if Cuba is ever to produce enough to feed its own population and break its reliance on food imports.

Land titles lie at the heart of any reconstruction project put forward by this generation of wealthy Cuban Americans. Juan Omar Sixto says his father lost five properties and a farm in Cuba's Pinar del Rio province to the revolution. While he insists he has no intention of removing any family living in those homes, he does want compensation for the nationalised land.
"I worked on that farm for five years of my life with my father, and they took it away. I want restitution or compensation. Even if they give me just a penny on the dollar, I'll take it."
"It's moral justice," he argues.

The Cuban government portrays such historic title claims as bitterness by a corrupt landed gentry who made fortunes on the backs of indentured workers and slaves. Both slavery and the system of indentured workers didn't end in Cuba until the late 19th Century.
The government also argues that the exiles could never stand that Castro passed land reforms which handed over their fields to the workers and the state.

"Most of our sugar mills have been dismantled, but we will recover those lands and put them into production," says Nicolás Gutiérrez, the president of the National Association of Sugar Mill Owners of Cuba, an exile organisation championing the title claims.
"I'm not promising it will be in sugar," he says.

"It might be in ethanol, co-generation, solar panels or water purification cells. Who knows? There are a lot of different options," he remarks. "We need to get them producing, we need to have a real wage paid to Cuban workers and create a multiplier economic effect across the island."

With the ice clinking in their drinks and a cool breeze rustling the palm trees on the perfectly manicured lawn, the CANCC members make it sound easy. But within hours of their gathering, Cuba had descended into its sixth nationwide blackout this year.
The disconnection between the hopes for change in Miami and the realities on the ground in Cuba is stark. Many Miami-based Cubans think the monumental shift they have prayed for is almost here.

If so, it will inevitably bring huge social and humanitarian disruption which the stricken island is ill-equipped to cope with. Even assuming the diaspora's support is well-intentioned rather than purely self-interested, fixing the island's failing electrical grid alone is estimated to cost $8bn to $10bn (£6bn to £7.5bn).

Before any industry in Cuba – from agriculture to tourism – can be revitalised by the exiles' wealth and political connections, Cubans continue to face acute shortages in food, water, fuel and medicines. Miami's ambitious plans aside, most Cubans just hope their days get a little easier sometime soon.
