articles.title: 'You used me': Teens tell judge how man lured them over Snapchat, as he pleads guilty
articles.summary: Three years after Hammad Shaikh lured and sexually assaulted underage girls he met on Snapchat, the 26-year-old pleaded guilty to seven offences and sat expressionless in a Calgary courtroom as…

image.caption: Hammad Shaikh, 26, pleaded guilty to offences involving the luring and sexual abuse of underage girls he targeted on Snapchat. (AP)

blocks.text: Calgary

Three years after Hammad Shaikh lured and sexually assaulted underage girls he met on Snapchat, the 26-year-old pleaded guilty to seven offences and sat expressionless in a Calgary courtroom as several of his victims delivered statements with what the judge described as “maturity, grace, kindness and bravery.”
Hammad Shaikh sentenced to 11.5 years in prison

Shaikh was mid-trial on 28 charges when he changed course and pleaded guilty to seven offences on Thursday involving victims between the ages of 12 and 16 years old. A publication ban protects the identities of the girls.
Justice Eleanor Funk accepted the prosecutors’ and defence lawyers’ joint proposal for an 11.5-year prison sentence.
“I hope you understand how damaging your conduct has been,” said the judge.

Details of Shaikh's crimes against the teens come from an agreed statement of facts prepared by prosecutors Sarah Goard-Baker and Stephanie Morton, and defence lawyers Rebecca Snukal and Mary Stephensen.
'I miss the person I was'
Several of the teenage girls, their loved ones and victim support workers were in court for Shaikh’s pleas and sentencing.
In a powerful and emotional display, three of the girls stood before their abuser in the courtroom and read aloud their victim impact statements.
“My view on intimacy is completely distorted now,” said VK, one of the girls lured and abused by Shaikh.

items: Trial begins for Calgary man accused of sexually assaulting underage girls he met on Snapchat

blocks.text: VK was 13 years old when Shaikh initiated contact over Snapchat. Their interactions lasted for months.
“I miss the person that I was before,” she said in court on Thursday.
“I really feel bad for my dad, though … I knew it would break his heart. I knew he would blame himself. None of it was his fault, nor was it mine.”
Victim had just lost parent
Court heard that in January 2024, Shaikh picked up VK, bought her flavoured vodka and marijuana and had sex with her in his car.
“I have no idea what my boundaries are because two years ago they were stomped on and run over," she said in court.
Another victim, LW, told the court that when she met Shaikh in the spring of 2023 she was “already hurting deeply from the loss of a parent.”
Shaikh gave LW alcohol and marijuana before he not only engaged in sexual activity with her in his car, but also recorded and saved videos of it.
'An immense amount of shame'
Shaikh admitted Thursday that he knew LW was 15 years old when he began messaging her on Instagram and Snapchat.
“I carried an immense amount of shame,” said LW. “I felt ashamed of every kiss, every touch, every word.”
“You used me in so many ways.”
More videos taken
In her statement, PC told the court that after she was victimized by Shaikh, she tried to take her own life.
Shaikh knew PC was 14 years old when he first made contact over Snapchat.
Over the next five months, he supplied marijuana and alcohol when the two met regularly and had sex in his car, home and a hotel room.
Shaikh again took videos that constituted child sexual abuse and exploitation material.
In the aftermath, PC said she suffered serious mental health issues, lost friends and stopped going to school.
“I smoked more weed and drank dangerous amounts to forget,” said PC. “I couldn't forgive myself.”
'A hurting child'
PC’s mother also read a statement, describing midnight ER visits and watching her daughter “wither away.”
“She could not be left alone … I had to focus on keeping my child alive,” said PC’s mother.
“A hurting child hurts the whole family.”
After Shaikh was first arrested, he was released on bail on conditions including that he have no contact with his victims and stay away from social media.
But Shaikh bought a new iPhone and contacted more girls.
Witness tampering
One of the charges he pleaded guilty to was luring. The victims of that offence are seven named complainants and eight unnamed, underage girls who police found evidence of on Shaikh’s new cellphone.
He also pleaded guilty to witness tampering.

Three months after his arrest, Shaikh contacted one of his victims and attempted to convince her to go to police and recant her complaint against him. He also tried to convince her that what happened between them was legal.
When given the chance to address the court, Shaikh stood up in the prisoner's box and apologized to his victims and his family.
"At the time, I failed to recognize the harm I caused to my victims," he said. "I will never truly know the extent of your pain ... I am terribly sorry to each and every one of you."
In her final words, Funk wished Shaikh luck in turning his life around after his prison term.
"What you do in that next chapter of your life will in part be up to you," said the judge.
"Through your own words, I am confident you are starting to realize the scope of damage."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Klopp wins first game as Germany coach, without 'top dogs'
articles.summary: It may have taken a little longer than he would have liked, but Jürgen Klopp has finally won a game as Germany coach. Despite a number of debutants, it was a familiar face who stood out in the…

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp has won his first game as Germany boss, after replacing Julian Nagelsmann after the World CupImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: After 47 days, three matches and 44 squad players, Jürgen Klopp has a first win as coach of Germany's men's fotball team. A straightforward 2-0 victory over Serbia in the Nations League on Thursday meant the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach avoided becoming the first Germany boss to win any of his first three games.
"I'm really happy today," Klopp told German public broadcaster ZDF. "We were outstanding when defending and when we had the ball. We simply played wonderful football."

Klopp had raised a few eyebrows by naming two squads for the four fixtures in this extended international window. But after a somewhat fortunate draw against the Netherlands and a shock loss to Greece with the more senior of the squads, it was left to those lower down the pecking order to get things going Thursday in Munich.
Bischof gets first goal on home turf

That meant a completely new starting XI and debuts to ‌goalkeeper Jonas Urbig ⁠and ⁠winger Derry Scherhant. Such players should "develop without the top dogs" Klopp said before the game. And while Urbig was untroubled by Serbia, his Bayern Munich teammate Tom Bischof made his mark by turning in the opener after Florian Wirtz, one of the sprinkling of senior players, hit the post. It was Bischof's first goal for Germany in only his second national team game.

blocks.caption: Florian Wirtz (left) and Tom Bischof were Germay's goalscorersImage: Karl-Josef Hildenbrand/AFP

blocks.text: "It's indescribable," said Bischof after the game at Bayern's Allianz Arena. "The stadium was on fire. I let it all out and was overjoyed." Unfortunately, he said, "my knees hurt a little from sliding on my knees. But that doesn't matter."

After a string of tournament failures, the latest new dawn for Germany comes with a little more patience. As well as Klopp's track record, there is a general acceptance from inside the country and abroad that Germany are no longer a top tier side.
"We're not the Bayern Munich of European football," Klopp said prematch. "We're a team that needs to find its footing."
Klopp: 'I liked everything'
While one win against a limited Serbia side will not change that, the emphatic nature of the performance impressed the new boss.

"I liked everything — the opening phase, the middle section, and the end. Our counter-pressing was off the charts," said the man whose Gegenpressing (Counter-pressing) tactic became his trademark at Dortmund. "We can afford to take all the liberties and risks we want when we win the ball back together. Everyone was there during our pressing moments."

The second half brought more debuts for players who may not have made a traditional 26-man squad. Cologne winger Said El Mala and Brentford's Vitaly Janelt made their Germany bows while Celtic's Mika Baur became the country's 1,000th men's international.
It was "surreal," Baur said. "Today was a highlight for everyone, not just for me with my debut."
Wirtz provides spark and hope

While Klopp may have seen enough from a few of the second string to afford them opportunities in the future, the performance of Liverpool midfielder Wirtz, who scored Germany's second goal, may be the most critical of the night.

Wirtz, 23, has struggled to find his best form in the Premier League and has blown hot and cold in his 47 caps for Germany. A cool and composed finish suggested that the player who was so highly regarded at Bayer Leverkusen can be coaxed to life by Klopp.

"It was loads of fun. Every single one of us gave it our all on the field. We stuck to the game plan and did almost everything right," said Wirtz, who took the captain's armband later in the game. "The players around me made it easy for me. We had a lot of movement in the middle. We were all fired up."

The challenge now for Klopp is to work out which of his wide pool of players are the ones he can rely on to take Germany to Euro 2028 and beyond. The next step is a chance for revenge against Greece in Thessaloniki on Sunday.

articles.title: US says Europe should ready fuel supplies as Trump threatens diesel ban
articles.summary: President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports in a bid to ease prices in the US ahead of the November elections.
articles.byline: Oliver Smith, Simon Jack, Archie Mitchell

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves as he mulls a ban on US exports of the fuel amid a global shortage.

The comments followed his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging for Europe to immediately ready and release such supplies. "American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar, he argued.
The US has threatened to restrict diesel exports amid surging costs due to the war in Iran. The issue is top of mind for US voters ahead of the crucial midterm elections.
On Thursday, Britain held talks with European partners about the potential release of diesel reserves in response to any ban.

The US is a vital supplier of diesel to the world, exporting between 1.2 and 1.5 million barrels per day, with experts warning a ban on shipments abroad could put further pressure on prices in other countries.
"We're thinking about it very seriously," Trump said of an export ban at the weekend.
On Thursday Trump added that he may ask European countries to release some of their diesel reserves, while Bessent said they should do so "immediately".

"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," Bessent said in a post on social media.

The plans come weeks ahead of November elections in the US, where control of Congress will be up for grabs. The president is set to travel across the US campaigning for Republicans in hopes of keeping control of the House and Senate.
Diesel prices in the UK hit record highs this week and are hovering just under 200p per litre, according to motoring organisation the RAC.
Britain's Energy Minister Martin McCluskey was on a call with European counterparts on Thursday to discuss the potential ban.

A source familiar with the discussions told the BBC it was prudent to prepare a co-ordinated response with other countries, including those across EU, but added that there were still European reserves left from a coordinated release of strategic fuel stocks earlier in the year.

"We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry," a government spokesperson said. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages, though prices are expected to rise further.
A European Commission spokesperson said today that there were "lots of calls, lots of meetings" taking place on the diesel situation, including with "high level contacts" in the US administration.

Prices of petrol and diesel globally have skyrocketed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war in Iran in February. The closure of the vital Strait of Hormuz, which typically transports around a fifth of the world's oil and gas, has pushed up the price of products made from oil.
An export ban from Russia, also a major supplier of diesel, has added to the pressure on prices.

Trump has argued that keeping any surplus barrels of diesel in the US would lower pump prices domestically, offering immediate relief to drivers, truckers, and businesses ahead of the midterm elections.
But David Fyfe, chief economist at Argus Media, said cutting off American supply would likely cause international prices to skyrocket.
Diesel prices have hit an all-time high in the UK, with the latest RAC figures showing average pump prices at 199.79p per litre, up from 142.38p
Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.
The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.
There were 15.1 million diesel vehicles on UK roads at the end of June, according to the Department for Transport. That is a drop from 15.7 million a year before.
There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

articles.title: Judge denies defence request to declare Lindsay Clancy not guilty
articles.summary: The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defence motion that had argued there wasn't enough evidence to prove she was responsible for…

image.caption: Lindsay Clancy is seen attending a hearing in a Plymouth, Mass., court earlier this week. (Greg Derr/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case on Thursday refused to declare her not guilty, turning down a defence motion that had argued there wasn't enough evidence to prove she was responsible for killing her three children.
Judge says prosecutors provided adequate evidence for jury to decide if Clancy is responsible
WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and attempted suicide.

During Clancy's first trial, which ended Sept. 4 with a deadlocked jury, her defence argued that she was not criminally responsible because of a mental disease, specifically a rare condition called postpartum psychosis. As such, the defence didn't dispute that the 36-year-old former labour and delivery nurse carried out the killings at her family's Massachusetts home in 2023.

However, in a hearing earlier this week, Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington tried to persuade the judge that prosecutors had not offered any proof that Clancy did it. Prosecutors argued there was plenty of evidence, calling Reddington's claim "laughable."

In his ruling, Judge William Sullivan noted that, for the purposes of his decision, he was required to analyze the evidence in the light most favourable to prosecutors — and that it was up to the jury, not the judge, to decide whether to believe expert witnesses for the defence who testified that Clancy was not responsible for her actions because of mental illness.
"There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Sullivan wrote.
Mental health problems acknowledged in trial

At the first trial, prosecutors acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems that included months of treatment and a stay in a psychiatric hospital, but argued that she knew what she was doing when she strangled the children — the youngest just eight months old — then tried to kill herself.
Sullivan had declared a mistrial with the jury split 11 to 1 in favour of acquitting Clancy of murder charges.
The Lindsay Clancy trial and maternal mental health

In Tuesday's hearing, Reddington suggested the entire case "was based on speculation" and proceeded to list the shortcomings in the prosecution's case. There was almost no police investigation, he claimed, and significant questions revolving around Clancy's condition outside the night of the killings and her lack of memory of what happened.

At the trial, jurors heard testimony that Clancy said she heard voices instructing her to kill Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and eight-month-old Callan Clancy. Her DNA was found on exercise bands used to strangle them. Before the trial, Reddington himself filed a motion in which he said Clancy was willing to stipulate, in writing, to her involvement in the children's deaths.

"For the first time, the defendant is arguing that there is no evidence she did this," prosecutor Shanan Buckingham told the judge. "I'd suggest to you the entire record is voluminous as to information supporting the fact that she did this."
No decision yet on possible 2nd trial
Clancy remains charged with murder and is expected to stay at a psychiatric hospital until her case is resolved.

Prosecutors have yet to decide whether to bring the case to trial for a second time. They could choose to retry her on first-degree murder charges or seek to try her only on lesser charges, including second-degree murder or manslaughter, or drop the case entirely.
Clancy could have been sentenced to life in prison if convicted of murder. If acquitted, the judge could have ordered her confined to a mental health facility.

Her former husband, Patrick Clancy, who discovered the children's bodies, has said in interviews that he forgives her for the killings. The livestreamed trial generated intense public interest and drew attention to maternal mental health after childbirth.
If you or someone you know is struggling, here's where to look for help:

items: Canada's Suicide Crisis Helpline: Call or text 988.
Provincial and territorial mental health support.
Kids Help Phone: 1-800-668-6868. Text 686868. Live chat counselling on the website.
This guide from the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health outlines how to talk about suicide with someone you're worried about.

Follow the day’s news live.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 13m agoOnline gaming 'shortcomings' put children at risk, eSafety report finds

blocks.text: Atlassian enters 10-year solar energy deal with community co-op to power Sydney HQ

A solar farm owned by a group of community investors has secured a 10-year deal with one of Australia’s biggest technology companies to help power its headquarters, Australian Associated Press reports.
Atlassian announced its virtual power purchase agreement with the Goulburn Community Energy Co-operative on Friday in a deal that will fund almost 70% of the project’s output over the next decade.

Electricity generated by the project in NSW’s Southern Tablelands will help to meet the renewable energy needs of the tech firm’s 39-storey Sydney base, currently in construction near Central station, when it opens in 2028.

The announcement comes amid heated debate over whether technology companies should be required to invest in renewable energy generation to meet growing demands from data centres and artificial intelligence operations in Australia.

The solar and battery farm, located on 2.2 hectares of industrial land in Goulburn, features 2,300 solar panels and a four megawatt-hour battery. Owned by a group of about 288 local investors, who contributed a minimum of $400, the farm connected to the electricity grid in March 2026, 12 years after it was proposed.
The agreement follows a $2.3m NSW government grant and would support local workers and suppliers, Andrew Bray, the Goulburn Community Energy Co-operative chair, said:

double quotation markOur active volunteers and investor community worked patiently and diligently across a number of years to see this project come to fruition. To have a blue-chip Australian company like Atlassian come on board as a commercial partner is a huge vote of confidence in what we have built.
Online gaming 'shortcomings' put children at risk, eSafety report finds

blocks.caption: Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Sarah Basford Canales
Online gaming services are failing to take enough action to prevent children being exposed to harmful content, a new report from the eSafety Commissioner has found.
In a report published today, the online safety watchdog found measures adopted by gaming providers were not up to standard and varied in quality between platforms.
Platforms with the dominant purpose of gaming are not covered under Australia’s under-16s social media ban but are subject to the eSafety Commissioner’s information gathering notices.
The report – which drew details from Fortnite’s developer, Epic Games, Roblox, Minecraft and Valve’s Steam – found some positive signs but overall determined “disparities and shortcomings”.

Among them, examples of some platforms relying on age self-declaration resulting in children being able to easily access third-party content lacking sufficient content moderation as well as a limited number of human moderators to respond to harmful content.
The commissioner, Julie Inman-Grant, said:

double quotation markWhile we have seen some safety improvements as a result of sustained regulatory pressure, including the recent court-enforceable undertakings we accepted from Roblox, there is still significant work to be done across the board to prevent serious harms in online gaming to children.
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

articles.title: Driver in crash that killed 2 Tsawwassen First Nation elders released from hospital: police
articles.summary: Police said Wednesday that the male driver of the vehicle may have suffered a medical emergency in the moments leading up to the crash on Wednesday. They did not elaborate on what that medical…

image.caption: First responders are pictured outside Tsawwassen Mills on Wednesday. Police say the investigation into a crash that killed 2 people, and injured 2 others, continues on Thursday. (Johna Baylon/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia·Updated

Police said Wednesday that the male driver of the vehicle may have suffered a medical emergency in the moments leading up to the crash on Wednesday. They did not elaborate on what that medical emergency was.
2 more people in hospital in critical condition, police say

The driver of a vehicle that struck and killed two Tsawwassen First Nation elders, and injured two other people, on Wednesday received medical attention following the crash and has been released from hospital.

At about 10:25 a.m. PT on Sept. 30, police say a vehicle struck four pedestrians outside Tsawwassen Mills mall, where a National Day for Truth and Reconciliation event was taking place. Two were killed, while two others were taken to hospital.

In an update on Thursday, police say the two people taken to hospital remain in critical condition, with "serious, life-altering injuries," according to Delta Police Department Staff Sgt. Mike Whiteley.
The identities of those killed in Wednesday's tragedy are not being released — however, Whiteley said the deceased were Tsawwassen First Nation elders.
The two people who were injured are not members of the Tsawwassen First Nation, Whiteley added.

items: 2 elders from Tsawwassen First Nation killed in crash at Truth and Reconciliation Day event

blocks.text: "This was a very tragic event," Whiteley told reporters at a news conference on Thursday afternoon.
"It was very difficult for our first responders, but also for our community, and especially for the Tsawwassen First Nation."
Police said Wednesday that the male driver of the vehicle may have suffered a medical emergency in the moments leading up to the crash. They did not elaborate on what that medical emergency was.
Police provide update on fatal Tsawwassen Mills collision
On Thursday, they said the driver received medical attention, and was released from hospital Wednesday afternoon.
"At this time, there is no information to suggest the collision was intentional," Delta Police said in its Thursday news release.
Video from the scene of the crash on Wednesday shows a pickup truck with the logo for the company Alpine Building Maintenance printed on its side.
In a statement Thursday, the company confirmed one of its vehicles was involved in the collision.
"We are co-operating with the appropriate authorities to support their investigation. Our thoughts are with everyone affected," it said.
Tsawwassen crash a tragic turn of events for community: councillor
No charges have been sworn as of Thursday afternoon, police said.
"If the evidence warrants us forwarding charges to Crown counsel, then we'll be doing that," Whiteley said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and leaders on the B.C. election campaign trail — David Eby, Emily Lowan and Lorne Doerkson — expressed their condolences to the families and the First Nation after the crash on Wednesday.

The Indian Residential School Survivors Society said in a post on social media that the loss of the two "beloved" elders is devastating, while the Huu-ay-aht First Nations on Vancouver Island said it feels the tragedy deeply as an elder who died was a grandparent of one of its citizens.
In a statement issued Thursday, the Tsawwassen First Nation requested privacy as it grieved the loss of the two elders, adding that its offices would be closed on Oct. 1 and 2.

"Two beloved [elders] from our community lost their lives. Our hearts are with their families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss. We are also holding close in our thoughts those who were injured and everyone who witnessed this tragedy," the statement reads.

"We recognize the profound impact this tragedy has had on our community as a whole. During this incredibly difficult time, we are grateful for the care, compassion, and support that has been extended to Tsawwassen First Nation."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Courtney Dickson is a journalist with CBC News based in Vancouver, covering stories throughout B.C. She has previously worked for CBC in Kamloops and Toronto. She has won Radio Television Digital News Association awards locally and nationally, and in 2022, won a Webster Award.

articles.title: Edmonton man charged for alleged death threat against Mark Carney: RCMP
articles.summary: Police arrested a 44-year-old Edmonton man accused of threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney, RCMP say.

image.caption: Police say they arrested a 44-year-old man from Edmonton, who's suspected of threatening the life of Prime Minister Mark Carney.

blocks.text: Edmonton
Police arrested a 44-year-old Edmonton man accused of threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney, RCMP say.
'Criminal online actions have real-world consequences,' RCMP say
Police arrested an Edmonton man accused of threatening to kill Prime Minister Mark Carney, RCMP say.

Dwight Peter MacIntyre, 44, has been charged with uttering a death threat against Carney, following alleged social media activity last month, according to a Thursday news release from the RCMP Federal Policing Northwest Region’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team (INSET).

“People should not assume they can make threats online without consequences. When online comments cross the line into criminal conduct, police will investigate and take appropriate action to hold those responsible accountable,” Supt. Matt Johnson, officer in charge of national security with RCMP Federal Policing Northwest Region, said in the news release.
“Criminal online actions have real-world consequences, regardless of whether they are made behind a screen.”

Police said INSET started investigating on Sept. 4, after RCMP became aware of a user on X, formerly known as Twitter, who had allegedly posted threats targeting the prime minister. RCMP didn't provide additional details about the alleged threats.
On Sept. 9, five days after the investigation started, INSET officers arrested and charged MacIntyre in relation to the incident, RCMP said.

Police didn't say where the arrest happened. But in Thursday's statement, INSET officials thanked the Edmonton Police Service and the Alberta RCMP’s Parkland detachment for their support in the investigation.
MacIntyre is scheduled to appear at the Alberta Court of Justice in Edmonton on Nov. 25.
In Thursday's statement, RCMP warned "this is a time for increased vigilance," as the security environment in which public figures operate continues to evolve within Canada and abroad.
MacIntyre is not the first person to have allegedly threatened Carney since he took public office more than a year ago.
A Calgary man was arrested and charged last month, in connection with allegations he threatened to kill Carney. Two men in Quebec were also arrested earlier this year on similar allegations.

articles.title: UK police make another arrest in RAF Fairford case
articles.summary: Counter terrorism police said a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. Five men arrested on Sunday remain on bail.

image.caption: The latest arrest comes after five British nationals were detained on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism on SundayImage: Ben Birchall/PA Wire/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police in the United Kingdom on Thursday said that another man had been arrested as part of the investigation into Sunday's security incident at a US-run air base in Gloucestershire.

The arrest of the dual UK-Iranian national came after British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the BBC there were "strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford."
Iran's embassy in London earlier said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation it was involved while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree."
What police have said
Counter terrorism police said that a 27-year-old dual UK-Iranian national was arrested in London "on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006."
They said that a second man who is a UK national was also questioned under caution and that searches of two properties had taken place.

"The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry," said Counter Terrorism Policing's Vicki Evans.

"As we've made clear, we're looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement. I'd like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation," Evans said.
UK releases air base plot suspects
Sunday's events at RAF Fairford

Five men in their 20s, all from the London area and with British citizenship, were arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terror offenses close to the RAF Fairford air base, which has been used by American bombers to strike Iran.
They were wearing face coverings.
Police seized three "suspicious" white vans and evacuated around 85 households in the vicinity, bringing in bomb disposal teams.
Police said a quantity of petrol was but no explosive devices were found in the vans.
The suspects have since been released on bail in a move questioned by US President Donald Trump.
Trump says RAF Fairford suspects known to US authorities

articles.title: Brazil attorney general says meddling ‘cannot be tolerated’ after Trump funding plans revealed
articles.summary:
Jorge Messias calls Guardian report ‘an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty’, as nation prepares to go to polls

Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro, Andrew Roth and Joseph Gedeon in Washington

blocks.text: Brazil’s attorney general has said foreign meddling in his country’s institutions and democracy “cannot be tolerated” after a Guardian report revealed how the Trump administration was pushing to direct funds to a campaign against the Brazilian supreme court.

Writing on X, Jorge Messias called the report “an important alert for Brazilian sovereignty”. “The information is especially serious in light of Brazil’s electoral process and the recent episodes of external pressure on our institutions,” Messias added.

Brazil is three days away from its presidential election – the outcome of which Washington has been accused of trying to influence – where the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, will face off against his far-right rival, the Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro. The pair are neck and neck in the polls.
According to the Brazilian television network GloboNews, the attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a criminal complaint to investigate potential wrongdoing, in response to the Guardian story.

Last year, the Trump administration used a campaign of sanctions and tariffs in a failed attempt to pressure Lula’s government and the supreme court over the coup trial of Bolsonaro’s father, the ex-president Jair Bolsonaro. Trump called Bolsonaro’s prosecution a “witch-hunt”, but he was convicted and handed a 27-year sentence for trying to seize power after losing the 2022 election to Lula.

In recent months, the Trump administration has again been accused of meddling in Brazilian affairs by using tariffs and the designation of two Brazilian organised crime groups as foreign terrorist organisations to boost Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign and weaken Lula.

Writing on Thursday, Messias said: “Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations. What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.”

Messias added: “It is the right of each generation of Brazilians to freely decide their destiny, protect their institutions, and hand over to their children a country that does not accept decisions about Brazil being made outside of Brazil. Our democracy belongs to Brazilians. And so it must remain.”

The attorney general’s comments came in response to a report that the Trump administration was pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa and the campaign against Brazil’s supreme court.
A $1m award titled “Countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court.
Bolsonaro’s far-right movement considers the supreme court – and in particular justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw Jair Bolsonaro’s trial – its greatest foe.

Moraes is widely seen to have played a key role in thwarting Jair Bolsonaro’s authoritarian plot, which culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília, despite concerns about the judge overstepping his constitutional authority in his crusade to protect democracy.
During the rightwing riots, hardcore Bolsonaro supporters trashed the presidential palace, congress and supreme court. The court sustained the most severe damage.
Bolsonaro supporters continue to claim their leader’s imprisonment is unjust and that he is the victim of a politically motivated sham driven by a corrupt “judicial dictatorship”.

Their criticism of Moraes and the supreme court has been bolstered by a recent scandal linking several judges, including him, to Daniel Vorcaro, the playboy banker at the centre of Brazil’s biggest banking scandal. Vorcaro has also been linked to the Bolsonaro family.

The banker reportedly gave the family more than £9m, supposedly to produce a biopic about Jair Bolsonaro starring Jim Caviezel, who played Jesus in Mel Gibson’s film The Passion of the Christ. On the eve of Vorcaro’s arrest last November, Flávio Bolsonaro messaged him to say: “Brother, I’ll always be with you.”

Vorcaro is being held in federal police custody in Brasília. His legal team has consistently denied wrongdoing. On Wednesday, his lawyers said he was not involved in “any kind of illicit activity or criminal practice”.

articles.title: Putin warns West that Russia is ready to use every weapon to protect Kaliningrad
articles.summary: Vladimir Putin insists Moscow is "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders.

blocks.text: Vladimir Putin has said Russia will use all weapons at his disposal if it considers it has come under direct attack in its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad.

Addressing the Valdai foreign policy forum, Putin insisted Russia was "not threatening anyone" and merely responding to statements by Western leaders that Moscow was preparing for war in 2029 or 2030.

Throughout this week, Russia has accused Nato of preparing to blockade its territory, which borders Lithuania and Poland, warning that it would even be prepared to use nuclear weapons if the West tried to cut off Kaliningrad from the rest of Russia.
Nato has sought to calm the situation, stressing it is a defensive alliance and urging Moscow to stop its "nuclear threats".
Western allies have faced a surge in so-called hybrid warfare incidents blamed on Russia, particularly in Poland and the Baltics in recent months.

Last week alone Poland said a Russian helicopter had strayed into its territory adjacent to Kaliningrad and Lithuania said its population felt "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said on Thursday that his country was preparing for further hybrid attacks, "including serious ones", after a drone armed with explosives was found in August on the tarmac at Leipzig airport close to Ukrainian cargo planes.
In a wide-ranging speech, the Russian leader told his audience he believed that international conflicts were highly likely to continue, but would get better as "Western hegemony" weakened.

Although Putin himself began the full-scale war in Ukraine in February 2022, he again blamed the West for provoking the invasion, arguing that it had simply been forced to defend itself and take up arms.
He also insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries, and on its ships in the Black Sea.
"Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," he said.

Putin admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helped the Kremlin finance the war.

Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since the war on Ukraine started in 2022. Other civilian infrastructure is also regularly hit, and a key bridge in Kyiv was attacked by drones on Thursday.
Putin also accused the West of instigating other conflicts.

"If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation, in this case we are talking about Kaliningrad but possibly some other territories, of course the issue of use by the Russian Federation of all arms at the disposal of our country will inevitably and immediately be on the agenda," he said.

He accused Nato of holding naval manoeuvres in the Baltic Sea which he argued represented serious threats to Kaliningrad. If the territory came under Western blockade, he said Russia would be prepared to use all means and forces, including nuclear.

"We are not threatening anyone. We do not intend to attack anyone in 2029, in 2030, in 2050. But if we come across an aggression we will have to respond. Citizens of European countries should be fully aware of that."
He added that while he was aware of the nuclear capabilities of countries such as the UK and France, the weapons at its disposal were unparalleled.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte made clear on Wednesday that none of the alliance's "exercises or activities" posed any threat to Moscow and the Kremlin's messaging was "absolutely not called for and not helpful".

Putin spent some time talking about leading countries in the world having armaments at their disposal that could "swipe away all life or at least push the Earth to catastrophic consequences", and said unfortunately no-one could be sure they would never be used.
He drew the analogy of a gun sitting on a theatre stage - if it was hanging there at the start of the show, it would certainly fire at the end.
He appeared to call for the rules of warfare to be rewritten, and warned of the increasing risk of artificial intelligence.
"The automation and digitalisation of warfare leads to its gamification. This leads to degradation and sliding back of humanity to barbarity," he said.

articles.title: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week
articles.summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, CBC's Johanna Wagstaffe shares the vibe at New York Climate Week, and what she learned from meteorologists there; we map out Canada's progress on…

image.caption: Grabbing a quick moment outside the WNYC radio studio before heading in to record. (Johanna Wagstaffe/CBC)

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hi, it's Johanna. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the weather we experience every day. But after spending Climate Week in New York with fellow meteorologists from across North America, one thing is clear: this job is getting deeply personal.
This week:

items: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week
The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals
Mycelium with your meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs

blocks.text: What I learned from North America's top meteorologists at Climate Week

I was invited to join a closed-door workshop in New York City during Climate Week called "Beyond the Forecast: How Trusted Weather Voices Can Help Communities Understand Climate and Extreme Weather." Hosted by the Clinton Global Initiative in partnership with the Eleven Eleven Foundation, the session offered a rare space to talk openly with other broadcast meteorologists about how we communicate climate change.

I mean, this is my bread and butter. For almost two decades, I've been talking about climate change through the everyday weather we experience. I've been grateful to have the support, platforms and formats at CBC to do just that.

Even so, there is a distinct weight to this work — seeing the data play out in real time, knowing the severity of a storm's impact before it hits, and navigating how politicized the term "climate change" has become. Stepping into my new role as the host of CBC's climate podcast What on Earth?, the timing couldn't have been better for this gathering.
Finding common ground in New York

Arriving in New York, I loved being recognized by fellow Canadians at Newark Airport — climate advisers from Vancouver headed to the same gathering. It was a nice reminder of why these conferences matter. Bringing people together (despite the carbon footprint of travel) creates a momentum you can't replicate virtually.

Walking from the subway up 5th Avenue toward the conference centre on my first day, I instinctively fell into the fast-paced ebb and flow of the city street. I credit my former Toronto days for my defensive walking skills, but adopting that rhythm makes you feel immediately plugged in. This trip was going to be all about feeling part of something bigger.

The workshop itself was one I won't soon forget. Nearly every major meteorologist I've watched on U.S. networks was there (plus Bill Nye!). Our scheduled two-hour session ran long — after all, we talk for a living — but it was deeply cathartic. Hearing forecasters from Fox News to CNN to ABC, alongside scientists and policy-makers, open up about the shared challenges of communicating climate risk felt like a rare moment of unity.
Here are a few takeaways I can share:
1. The connection between weather and climate is undeniable — but the pushback is real
Underlying every discussion in that room was one overarching reality: we are all trying to talk about climate change as station scientists.

The science behind extreme weather is indisputable. But for television forecasters attempting to bring that science into daily broadcasts, the pushback from audiences can be tough — and deeply emotional. While I've been lucky enough to avoid the absolute worst of it, let's just say you never truly develop a thick skin. And knowing what lies ahead when forecasting a devastating storm carries a real weight.

Between sessions, I raced from Midtown down to SOHO to record in the studios at WNYC (New York public radio) — a fun moment of solidarity, hopping from one public broadcaster's home base to another. But the conversation I recorded hit home sharply. I spoke with forecaster Chris Gloninger, who made the difficult decision to leave his TV news career after facing severe harassment and a death threat simply for explaining climate links on air.

But Chris's story was a stark reminder that serving as a trusted voice often comes at a high personal cost. To go "beyond the forecast," weather communicators need more than just thick skin — we need strong community support to keep having these vital conversations safely.
2. U.S. and Canadian TV live in different broadcast universes

I attended the workshop alongside only one other Canadian: my friend Mark Robinson from The Weather Network, who I went to meteorology school with! Being there together highlighted how much the U.S. and Canada have in common, and also just how differently our two media markets operate.

American broadcast TV remains deeply traditional, with millions of viewers still tuning in to local 6 o'clock newscasts every night. For U.S. forecasters, that means trying to cram complex climate attribution science into a lightning-fast, two-minute weather window between commercial breaks.

At CBC, as the media landscape has shifted, we've chosen to experiment with meeting audiences where they are. Beyond dedicated space on podcasts like What On Earth? and digital platforms, our local TV markets frequently carve out extra airtime specifically to connect the dots between severe weather and climate change. Having that room to explain why a heat wave or atmospheric river is happening is something I was reminded not to take for granted — because in a tight TV hit, context is often the first thing left on the cutting-room floor. But as more U.S. newsrooms experiment with climate-dedicated segments and digital extras, the potential to inform communities is huge. It shows that when we give trusted weather voices room to breathe, audiences gain a far better understanding of the world shifting around them.

Stepping out of those closed-door rooms in New York, I was reminded that connecting those dots on air isn't always easy, and it certainly isn't always comfortable — but as extreme weather becomes our daily reality, it's a conversation we're more committed than ever to having.
— Johanna Wagstaffe
Old issues of What on Earth? are here. The CBC News climate page is here.

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode: When a meteorologist took a job in Iowa, he was excited to make his forecasts matter to viewers by bringing in climate impacts that were relevant to their lives, like rising costs and energy independence. But then the backlash began, escalating to a death threat.

He's not the only one. At climate week in New York City, a group of meteorologists gathered to share stories about speaking to often polarized audiences. When facts become political, how can climate change's frontline communicators stick to the science?

What On Earth? drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen. The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.
Reader feedback
Last week, we told you about a unique air quality meets wearable art project that's trying to bring awareness about dangerous pollutants especially when we can't see them.

Edwina Hylton wrote in with an important point: "In the eventuality that the device shows serious pollution, what is the person wearing the device supposed to do? Fine to know things are bad, but if there isn't a reasonable alternative, what is the point in collecting the information?"
While not always equitable or within reach, some experts we've spoken to over the years have said awareness gives a power of choice to take action, like wearing a mask or moving indoors.
And, for some, like reader Maureen Moffat, awareness is a click away. She writes, "I check the air quality daily on the net. Easy."
Got questions, comments, or just want to share something? Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)
The Big Picture: Progress on the world's nature goals

Four years ago, Canada welcomed negotiators from around the world to strike a historic deal on protecting nature. The conference was supposed to be in China, but it was 2022 and the COVID-weary government there had decided not to host.

So the meeting reverted to Montreal, which hosts the secretariat of the UN treaty that governs biological diversity, and I jumped on a train to go cover it. Canada led negotiations to land a new global target: protecting 30 per cent of lands and oceans by 2030. And it decided to lead by example by embarking on its own ambitious conservation agenda.
Here's a map of Canada's protected spaces. Canada has protected about 14 per cent of its lands and 15.5 per cent of its oceans so far.

And a new assessment says there's progress internationally — the world will reach 27 per cent protection on land by 2030. For oceans, protection will only reach 12 per cent. I spoke to Steven Guilbeault, Canada's former environment minister and the guy who helped land that deal in Montreal, about why we are falling short — and also why he's still optimistic countries will ramp up the fight against biodiversity loss.
— Inayat Singh
Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

items: A man in Squamish, B.C., has put his Halloween zombie decoration out early — to keep bears out of his garbage bins. See how the bears are responding in this CBC News video.

Kids are being toilet trained later and later. That's costing parents in money spent on diapers and time spent on additional gross diaper changes. But it's also creating a lot more plastic waste. A new study calculates the environmental cost, and offers some solutions.

Mountainous, densely populated Japan doesn't have many places to put large solar farms, but it has found a solution in a type of infrastructure that proliferated in the economic boom of the 1980s and is now disused.
A new study shows electric trucks are becoming cheaper to operate than their diesel counterparts and how quickly the savings can outstrip the higher up-front cost in some European countries.

Canada's Building Canada Strong Act is supposed to speed up infrastructure projects. But it could also dismantle environmental safeguards that protect Canadians and prevent wildlife from extinction, despite the federal government claiming otherwise, environmental groups tell CBC's David Thurton and Olivia Stefanovich.

blocks.text: Mycelium meatballs? How one Vancouver company is farming fungi to combat meat costs
If fermented liquid fungus from a bioreactor doesn't sound like your idea of a delicious meal, the folks at Maia Farms say, don't knock it 'til you've tried it.
The Vancouver-based company has figured out a way to grow and harvest mycelium — the hidden, underground root-like networks of fungus that give rise to mushrooms.
"The bioreactor allows us to control the environment in which the mycelium are grown," said chief innovation officer Sean Lacoursiere.
"It allows us to keep everything moving and grooving and it also allows us to aerate and provide all the oxygen that the mushroom will need."
Company argues mushrooms could help lower skyrocketing meat costs for restaurants
The result is a food product that can be mixed with different protein sources to add bulk and enhance a meal's nutritional profile.
While mushroom products are often used in meat substitutes, one of Maia's target markets is the meat industry itself.
"We can add a lot of nutritional, taste and texture benefits while reducing the amount of meat that's required," Lacoursiere said.
The offering couldn't be timelier for restaurateurs and other food retailers struggling to keep costs down as the price of meat soars.
According to Canada Beef, retail beef averaged $28 per kilogram in April, up 15 per cent from a year ago and close to a record high.
Maia Farms' director of food science and innovation Karen McAfee said mycelium could replace between 25 and 40 per cent of the meat in items like sausage rolls, meatballs and burger patties.
"It can help retain moisture… it can also help with the high level of umami flavour," she said.
Better for the planet
The benefits of hiding mushrooms in your meat go beyond the financial.
"From our estimates, we produce around two kilograms of carbon dioxide per kilogram of material," Lacoursiere said.
According to a 2024 report by the Canadian Roundtable for Sustainable Beef, one kilogram of consumed boneless beef in Canada produces 32.8 kilograms of carbon dioxide.
The same amount also requires 1,912 litres of water, almost four times the 500 litres Maia reports in its process.
"I don't think people really comprehend just how much of a difference this type of product can make," he said.
Finding consumers
While meat alternatives are readily available in Canadian supermarkets, sales in the sector have been declining for several years.
Lacoursiere is hoping Maia has what it takes to buck the trend.
"The whole goal of our company here is to produce mycelium at large scales, at a very cost competitive level. And we're already seeing that," he said.
As for the "ick" factor?
"It's an oyster mushroom. It's been eaten for hundreds, if not thousands of years. It's delicious. We just found a way to grow it in a submerged liquid state."
— Ruby Cornish

articles.title: Latvians head to the polls with Russia on their minds
articles.summary: On October 3, Latvians will elect a new parliament with Russia looming large over the campaign. Security fears dominate the agenda, but so does a debate over the economic cost of cutting ties with…

image.caption: Latvia goes to the polls for parliamentary elections on October 3, 2026.Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: Four German Air Force Eurofighter jets stand ready at Latvia's Lielvarde military air base, just 60 kilometers from Riga. The aircraft are part of NATO's efforts to strengthen Baltic air defenses on the alliance's eastern flank ahead. Germany sent the jets amid repeated drone incursions, which have put Latvia on alert ahead of the country's elections on October 3.
Security fears ahead of elections

Security has become one of the defining issues of this campaign — defense promises appearing on the programs of most of the leading parties in Latvia. And the Latvian public's anxieties aren't unfounded.

In recent months, several drones have entered Baltic airspace. The latest incident occurred on September 15 in Lithuania, when a drone believed to have crossed from Belarus was shot down by an NATO fighter jet.

On top of that there are hybrid threats, including migrant flows that Latvia and its neighbors say are being encouraged by Russia's ally Belarus to pressure the EU and test border security. Intelligence officials of several European countries, including Latvia and the Czech Republic have warned that Russia could seek to test NATO in the upcoming "months, not years."

blocks.caption: Guard on the Latvian-Russian border.Image: Gints Ivuskans/AFP

blocks.text: "There are concerns in the West and also here in the Baltic states that Russia might be trying some further actions here in the Baltics," says Maris Andzans, director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies in Riga. "If you want to test NATO, there is no better place than the Baltic states."
Near-unanimous agreement on defense

Latvia elects its 100-seat parliament, Saeima, through proportional representation, meaning coalition governments are the norm. Polls currently put the centrist United List, led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs ahead, followed by the populist alliance Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance and Latvia First led by Ainars Slesers. The center-left Progressives and the conservative National Alliance are also expected to enter parliament.
Most of these Latvian parties view Russia as a security challenge.

"The biggest threat is our neighbors, Russia and Belarus," says Agnese Kupca of the United List. "Our partners in the EU should understand: it is not only our border with Russia, but also EU and NATO border with aggressor."

Latvia is one of the few NATO members that have committed by law to spending 5% of GDP on defense, and analysts say the country's foreign policy orientation is unlikely to change regardless of which coalition emerges after the vote as there is nearly unanimous consensus on the importance of NATO. Which is backed by their voters: according to Friedrich Ebert Stiftung (FES) Security Radar 2025 Latvians generally have a positive view of NATO.

blocks.caption: Unites List election campaign poster featuring Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs before the general election in Riga, Latvia.Image: Ints Kalnins/REUTERS

blocks.text: Economic concerns among voters
But while security policy enjoys broad agreement, the economic consequences of Latvia distancing itself from Russia remain contentious.

Before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia was among Latvia's most important trading partners. Since 2022, Latvia has reduced imports from Russia and Belarus by more than 90% and introduced some of the toughest restrictions in the EU on goods from the two countries. Latvia's economy has adapted, but businesses with strong pre-war links to Russia were among the hardest hit.

"This closeness to the theater of war has strongly influenced the investment climate," says political analyst Filips Rajevskis. "So the big question is how to increase the investments and grow the economy."

Many Latvians reject any economic cooperation with Russia on security grounds. Sixty percent said they want Latvia to reduce dependence on Russia, according to FES Security Radar 2025. "In the current situation, it's absolute nonsense. We can't watch what's happening and still be friends with Russia," one passerby in Riga told DW.
Not breaking up with Russia completely?
At the same time 20% of Latvians, according to FES, favor closer ties with Russia. Calls for a more pragmatic approach towards its eastern neighbor are not uncommon in the political debates.
Julija Stepanenko, leader of Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Alliance, has repeatedly argued against completely severing economic ties with Russia and Belarus.

Earlier this year, it emerged that Stepanenko has received gifts worth roughly €400,000 ($470,000) from her father, a Russia-based businessman whose company manufactures construction materials, including anti-tank fortifications known as "dragon's teeth." But despite that, her party remains in second place in the polls.

When DW met Lyubov Shvetsova, one of Sovereign Power/Union of New Latvians party candidates at a campaign stand just outside the center of Riga, she rejected accusations that the party is pro-Russian.
"Our approach is pragmatism oriented toward the interests of Latvian business," she said.
Economic pragmatism
Another advocate of a more pragmatic economic approach is Ainars Slesers, former businessman and leader of Latvia First.
During an interview on Latvian public television earlier in September, Slesers argued that transit of goods with Russia should continue as long as it is not prohibited by EU sanctions.

His party has focused heavily on economic issues, arguing that Latvia should prioritize growth and investment over what it sees as excessive self-imposed restrictions. And this approach has found support: more than 9% are ready to vote for Latvia First, which is in third place in the polls.
However, discussions about fully restoring trade with Russia are premature, party member Edmunds Zivtins told DW. "As long as the war in Ukraine is ongoing, we cannot talk about it," he said.
Language and identity dividing Latvia
Analysts say such parties may attract some voters who feel alienated by Latvia's increasingly restrictive approach toward Russia.

blocks.caption: Golden roofs atop Saints Boris and Gleb Orthodox Cathedral are seen over trees in the centre of Daugavpils, eastern Latvia.Image: Wojtek Radwanski/AFP

blocks.text: The appeal is not necessarily driven by support for the Kremlin. Rather, it often comes from parts of the country's Russian-speaking minority who feel overlooked by mainstream parties and uneasy about policies such as the phase-out of Russian-language school education and the reduced role of Russian in public life.
About one-third of Latvia's population speaks Russian at home.
However, the outcome of these elections is hard to predict. Filips Rajevskis says many voters are hiding not only their party preference, but even their decision to go to vote ahead of elections.

As Latvians head to the polls, Moscow is shaping the campaign in ways both direct and indirect: as a security threat driving support for NATO and defense spending, and as an economic and cultural question that continues to divide parts of the electorate.

articles.title: France school protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ as PM calls crisis cabinet meeting
articles.summary:
About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents under way outside high schools around the country

A

blocks.text: A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned, as it said many schools would switch to online classes to protect teachers and pupils.

The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, called a crisis cabinet meeting on Thursday and told ministers to cancel travel plans to deal with the demonstrations, which erupted in the Paris region last week but have snowballed across the country.

Lecornu’s office said: “This upsurge in violence makes it virtually impossible to maintain the continuity of public education and is exposing staff and students to danger.” The education minister, Édouard Geffray, is to meet pupil representatives on Friday.

About 900 demonstrations, blockades and related incidents were under way outside high schools around the country, police said, with more than 160 shut down as a result. Access was also blocked to about 30 university campuses on Thursday, including in Paris and Marseille.

blocks.caption: The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves. Photograph: CLPress/Abaca/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Hundreds of lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 625 on Wednesday alone, the interior ministry said. More than 80 police and firefighters and 120 pupils and teachers have been injured.

The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.

Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles, with the interior ministry announcing an internal police investigation after accusations of excessive force and brutality by officers against three pupils.

Rubbish bins have been set on fire outside many schools and more serious arson attempts have been reported inside some buildings. Fire damage in one school in Nantes in the north-west was so extensive that it will stay closed for a month, authorities said.

blocks.caption: Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests. Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In the northern city of Caen, 16-year-old Maelle said she wished those setting bins on fire would protest “with words”. Students were protesting “against this government that doesn’t invest in heating, air conditioning, or teachers’ salaries”, she told AFP.

In Strasbourg in the north-east, tram services were temporarily suspended to “restrict the movements of rioters and demonstrators”, the regional prefect said, after protesting students obstructed the tracks with crowd control barriers.

“There are 35 of us per classroom,” one 17-year-old Strasbourg student said. “There aren’t enough toilets, and there are water leaks in some rooms. The building is falling apart, the cafeteria is too small. There’s zero budget, zero resources.”

Several bin fires were also reported in the southern city of Toulouse; while in Lille, young people wearing black hoodies destroyed a bus stop. In Marseille, there were attempts to light fires inside two schools. In one, a teacher was splashed with petrol.

blocks.caption: Injuries have mainly been from hurled objects but also from police-fired riot-control projectiles. Photograph: Miguel Medina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: While many teachers and several headteachers have reported being physically threatened and sometimes attacked, some support their pupils. Juliette Estiville, a high-school Spanish teacher in Paris, said that the police response had disgusted her.

“I’m actually here just to provide protection, to form a barrier between the police and the students,” she said. “Today went well, it’s going well, but I think that the teachers who come to the blockades are really there to protect our young people.”

The government has accused the radical left La France Insoumise (LFI) party of encouraging the protests, with several LFI MPs and mayors, including Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis, cheered at demonstrations.

The party’s candidate for the 2027 presidential election, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, insisted on Thursday that LFI backed “non-violent methods of struggle” and added that his “greatest worry is an unbearable level of police violence against these young people”.

articles.title: NAZA film-makers say they spoke to more than 100 sources about Israeli actions in Gaza
articles.summary:
Team behind documentary push back against IDF attempt to discredit its exposure of military systems

The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s…

blocks.text: The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary.

In its response, which the IDF said was based on statements made by the film-makers and a review made by a representative who had attended a viewing, the Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on interviews with two dozen intelligence and other troops who had only a partial picture of the target approval process.

At the centre of the IDF’s rebuttal was its often repeated claim that its rules of engagement explicitly distinguish between militants and civilians and prohibit deliberately targeting civilians, while requiring commanders to take steps to minimise civilian harm, claims that have long been challenged over the years by critics.
While acknowledging that it used AI to help recommend potential targets in Gaza, the IDF also said final decisions made on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.
The IDF also denied that it had approved, planned or carried out an attack anticipating 500 civilian casualties in pursuit of a single Hamas target.

The IDF statement follows previous efforts by Israeli politicians to dismiss NAZA – a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike – which have accompanied death threats against the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and calls by the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for them to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship.

It also echoed previous complaints by some Israeli critics – including journalists – that the film’s military sources were anonymised, despite the fact that source protection in media investigations is commonplace and regarded by much of the media as an ethical requirement.

“The film NAZA presents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal,” the statement added.

Responding to the IDF statement, the Guardian, which produced the film, disclosed further details of how the team had verified the allegations which involved scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.
A spokesperson said: “The IDF’s attempt to portray the 24 participants in NAZA as junior-ranking officers involved only in the early stages of the targeting process is false.
“They include officers and soldiers who were involved in multiple stages of the targeting process in Gaza, including intelligence, operations and the final authorisation process.

blocks.caption: People walk past the rubble of destroyed buildings in Jabaliya in the northern Gaza Strip. Photograph: Dawoud Abu Alkas/Reuters

blocks.text: “The process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.

“Over the past three years we have together interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes.

“The Guardian stands fully behind the film, which builds on three years of detailed reporting by the Guardian and our partners. Several highly respected news organisations have subsequently confirmed the IDF’s use of AI-driven systems in the Gaza offensive and the loosening of safeguards to protect civilians, including the New York Times, Washington Post and Associated Press.”

While Netanyahu has claimed that Israeli military safeguards have led to one of the lowest civilian-combatant ratios in modern warfare, that has been challenged by the IDF’s own leaked casualty assessments, by the UN’s commission of inquiry in 2024 and research by NGOs including Action on Armed Violence.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea sever ties amid Tigray fighting
articles.summary: Ethiopia said it was expelling Eritrean diplomats in response to Eritrea's "direct and indirect acts of hostility." Eritrea said it had "no choice but to reciprocate in kind."

image.caption: Ethiopia's foreign ministry said the Ethiopian diplomats posed a 'direct threat' to national security [FILE: July 7, 2026]Image: Office of the Prime Minister-Ethiopia

blocks.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties on Thursday after Ethiopia accused its northern neighbor of involvement in renewed fighting in the Tigray region.

The Ethiopian Foreign Ministry was the first to announce that it was shutting its embassy in Eritrea "in response to Eritrea's direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia."
The Ethiopian embassy ​in Eritrea had been reopened in 2018 as ​part of ⁠the rapprochement that culminated in Prime ⁠Minister ​Abiy Ahmed receiving the Nobel Peace Prize.

Ethiopia's Foreign Ministry also declared ten Eritrean diplomats "persona non grata", accusing them of "involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security." The Eritrean diplomats were given 48 hours to leave the country.
Hours later, Eritrea's Foreign Ministry called the move "absurd" and said the expulsion of ten of its diplomats from Addis Ababa had effectively shuttered its embassy there.
Eritrea said it therefore had "no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries ​that this entails."
Reports of earlier blast at Ethiopian military headquarters
The measures came following reports of an explosion overnight at Ethiopian military headquarters in Addis Ababa.

The AFP news agency reported that the explosion took place at the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) headquarters between midnight and 1:00am local time, citing diplomatic and security sources with the information.
The sources could not provide further information relating to the nature of the blast or who was responsible, or if there had been any casualties.
The Associated Press, citing security sources, reported that there had been three blasts that came after the government banned the use of drones in the capital.
It's not clear whether the blasts were related to any attack or whether they had been part of training exercises.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again

Eritrea has denied allegations that it supports an armed alliance — which includes the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the the Amhara Fano National Movement, and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) — currently fighting Ethiopian government forces. The coalition is named Alliance for Survival.
Hundreds have been killed and wounded since last week's resumption of heavy fighting in northern Ethiopia.
Clashes have been ongoing and have have taken place along several fronts.
The United Nations has called for de-escalation of the fighting and for talks between the government and the recently formed alliance.

articles.title: Britain in talks with European allies over release of emergency diesel stockpiles
articles.summary:
Ministers discuss drawing down EU countries’ reserves after Donald Trump threatens to cut off US supplies

Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles…

blocks.text: Britain is in talks with European allies over releasing emergency diesel stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.

Ministers held calls with counterparts from the European Commission, Germany, France, Italy and Ireland on Thursday to discuss whether to draw down reserves after the Trump administration told Germany and France to release their stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.

The warning, first reported by Reuters, marks an escalation of pressure on Europe as Trump considers a potential wider ban to help lower domestic fuel prices before the US midterm elections in November.

A US official told the news agency: “It is in Europe’s best interest to ⁠work with the United States as we pursue multiple pathways to boost the supply of refined products and lower costs for consumers.”
Martin McCluskey, the UK minister for local energy, was reportedly on the call with EU countries on Thursday.
The Trump administration has been frustrated with France and Germany for what it considers their not following through on commitments to release oil and petrol stocks.

Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices.

It was unclear whether the UK would be included in such a ban, but the loss of US supply would drive prices up sharply at the pumps because the UK does not refine enough diesel to meet domestic demand. About a third of UK diesel imports last year came from the US.
The average price of a litre of diesel in the UK hit a new all-time high on Wednesday of 199.72p, according to the motoring body the RAC.
John Healey, the chancellor, admitted earlier this week that UK diesel prices were “extreme” and said the government was in discussion with the US over trying to stop a ban.

The US war in Iran has disrupted energy supplies via the strait of Hormuz and sent the price of oil soaring. Before the war, in February, Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil prices – traded at about $72 a barrel. It was above $101 on Thursday.

Releasing more stocks would represent a problem for European countries, which need to balance the need to bring down domestic fuel prices with keeping high stocks for a potential worsening energy crisis over the winter if the Iran war continues.
after newsletter promotion

“The UK continues to need fuels – from transport to chemicals, agriculture and defence,” said Elizabeth de Jong, the chief executive of the trade group Fuels Industry UK. The latest US threat showed the UK “cannot solely rely on overseas production for domestic energy security”, she added.

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said on Wednesday that the US administration expected announcements from Europe soon regarding new diesel supplies. “We’ve lost some diesel exports from the Middle East, although we’re restoring ​those, and we’ve lost diesel exports ​from China,” he said. “So that’s ⁠a lot of interruptions.”
Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK energy secretary, has been in contact with Wright to raise concerns.

Trump has said he was “very seriously” considering a US diesel export ban to try to curb soaring prices, and has urged Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries over concerns that they could further push up prices. Russia had already extended its ban on diesel exports until the end of October after Ukrainian attacks on refining companies.
A government spokesperson said: “We have a diverse and resilient supply. We continue to engage with our international partners and the UK fuel industry.”
