It's only been six months since Canada's Jeremy Hansen made history by flying around the moon. Now, it's Joshua Kutryk's turn to blast off into space.
Kutryk and three fellow astronauts are launching to the International Space Station (ISS) today in a joint NASA-Space X mission. The crew will be living and working on the ISS for roughly six months.

"I never, ever, ever, ever … thought that I would have this opportunity to go out on behalf of Canada and do a mission like this," Kutryk, the flight's Canadian astronaut, said during a media call on Wednesday.

The crew will blast off inside SpaceX's Crew Dragon from Cape Canaveral, Fla. The launch was postponed from Sept. 12 due to an issue with the spacecraft, but Kutryk has said he has faith the vehicle is ready to fly.
The Crew-13 launch, as it's called, also includes NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteriatnikov.
The crew will join several astronauts who are already on station and will conduct several experiments, some of which are Canadian.

items: October 1A difficult jobNicole MortillaroHeather Kutryk at this morning's walkout. (Shawn Benjamin/CBC)Being an astronaut sounds pretty cool to some people (count me in!), but let’s not forget the challenges that come with that.You’re training for years, oftentimes with long hours and trips around the world. You also are waiting to find out when your mission will come up. It takes a lot of patience and drive.But then, finally, comes the day: Launch day. Imagine leaving everything you have ever known behind, especially your loved ones.Joshua Kutryk may be blasting off to live a dream, but he’s also leaving his wife — who is pregnant — and two children behind as he embarks on a dangerous mission.

Off to space, with a new baby on the wayVerity StevensonISS mission 'starting to feel real,' says wife of Canadian astronaut Joshua KutrykIt's t-minus two days before Alberta-born astronaut Joshua Kutryk heads to the International Space Station (ISS) in a joint NASA-SpaceX mission. Kutryk and his crew will join several astronauts who are already on the station and conduct experiments, some of which are Canadian.As the crew prepared for launch this week, they got to spend time with their families who were quarantining along with them in a hotel in Cape Canaveral, Fla. Heather Kutryk, Joshua Kutryk's wife, says she and the couple's two children, Anna, 5, and Peter, 7, have been enjoying trips to the beach with their dad before his six-month space odyssey. "It's just good quality family time leading up to the launch and I'm grateful for that," said Kutryk.Kutryk is pregnant and due to give birth in November during Joshua's mission. She said she isn't stressed about the delivery because of the strong community and support she has around her. "It was a bit of a surprise — not exactly planned, but you know, it's a great thing," she said, laughing. The family has lived in Houston since 2017, with Joshua training and preparing for this launch for years. He's undergone intense physical training, learned Russian and travelled to Los Angeles, Europe, Japan and Russia in preparation, his wife said.Anna and Peter also seem to be taking their father's departure in stride, although Peter has had his moments, his mother said. "Both Josh and Peter have a really special bond. So, I think it's hitting him a little bit harder. Anna, she's just independent. She's very strong-willed and she's just kind of like, 'All right, I'll see you later, Dad. We're good!'"Kutryk, too, says she feels OK about her husband's departure because it's been years in the making.Still, she said, "maybe it'll hit me when he's actually gone, but so far I feel like we're going to be great."

Who is Joshua Kutryk?Nicole MortillaroMeet Joshua Kutryk, the next Canadian to go to spaceNASA has announced that Expedition 75, the next crew to go to the International Space Station, will include Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk. Kutryk, NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov will spend several months aboard the ISS.Kutryk was born on March 21, 1982, in Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., where he was raised on a cattle farm. His interests include backcountry skiing, mountaineering, cycling and paragliding (sounds like he really likes being high up!).He's been a test pilot, a fighter pilot and is still a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force.In 2017, he was recruited by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) alongside Jenni Gibbons, who served as Jeremy Hansen's backup for the Artemis II mission around the moon back in April.He graduated from astronaut training in 2020 and was certified for capcom (short for "capsule communication," a term left over from the old NASA days) for the ISS.He's trained in caves, which tests astronauts' physical and mental endurance needed for long-duration space missions, and participated in a lunar geology expedition at the Mistastin Lake Impact Crater in Labrador.He was supposed to fly on Boeing's CST-100 Starliner capsule to the ISS; however Boeing has suffered major setbacks to their spacecraft. That mission will now be uncrewed. Instead, he's flying on the much-tested SpaceX Crew Dragon where he sits right now.

Meet your crewNicole MortillaroCanadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, left, U.S. astronaut Luke Delaney, U.S. astronaut Jessica Watkins, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov prepare to head to the SpaceX Dragon spacecraft in Cape Canaveral, Fla., this morning. (Marco Bello/AFP/Getty Images)Let's look at who makes up this Crew-13 launch.First, the name Crew-13 comes from the fact that it's SpaceX's 13th mission to be launched since NASA restarted flights from U.S. soil, following years of relying on the Russian space agency (Roscosmos) to get astronauts to the ISS. This happened after NASA cancelled its space shuttle program in 2011.While SpaceX and Boeing were both awarded contracts to build spacecraft to take astronauts to the ISS, so far only SpaceX has succeeded after Boeing suffered major setbacks.There are two NASA astronauts on this mission. Jessica Watkins is the spacecraft commander, and Luke Delaney is the pilot.Then there is Sergey Teteryatnikov from Roscosmos, who will be a mission specialist.And finally, we have our own Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency, who will also serve as a mission specialist.This will be the first flight for not only Kutryk, but also Delaney and Teteryatnikov.

Ready to goNicole MortillaroA Tesla vehicle awaits astronauts at the morning walkout. Three Teslas, including a Cybertruck, all had these same licence plates. (Shawn Benjamin/CBC)Before the crew head to their spacecraft for any mission, there is a traditional walkout from the quarantine building.Fences are put up around the area where the press gathers, but there’s a special area for the families and their astronaut escorts, who are all in quarantine. NASA administrator Jared Isaacman arrived and briefly went into the quarantine facility.There are a lot of photographers here, many of them old-timers who know the game and brought ladders to get the best view.Three Tesla cars were onsite to take the astronauts and others to the pad, all of which had licence plates that read "LUCKY 13." Because…you know.It was great to see Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques, who flew to the ISS in 2018, arrive with Kutyrk's daughter on his shoulders, while Kutryk's son and wife followed. His son pointed up towards the windows of the nearby building as NASA employees gathered at the windows. NASA employees don't seem to take these launches for granted.The Crew-13 astronauts soon walked out of the quarantine facility at 7:40 a.m., waving to the crowd and spending a few moments with their families.Kutryk's wife Heather was visibly moved, appearing to hold back tears and turn her face away. Eventually, the four astronauts entered their Teslas, and Joshua lowered his window as his son ran to give him a kiss.It was an emotional experience for us all.

Chances of favourable weather at launch: 40%John MazerolleA SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket with the company's Dragon spacecraft on top, on the launch pad at Space Launch Complex 40 yesterday at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. (Joel Kowsky/NASA/Getty Images)At last update, weather officials with the U.S. Space Force 45th Weather Squadron predicted a 40 per cent chance of favourable conditions at the launch pad for liftoff.There are a long list of weather criteria that must be met on launch day. NASA said this morning that the main concerns today are nearby cumulus clouds, cloud thickness and precipitation. Other non-weather related considerations need to be cleared before launch is ultimately given the green light.

articles.title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
articles.summary: "My family and I will not truly be safe as long as Putin is in power," says the former chess world champion.

blocks.text: An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.
Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.

His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.

Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.

Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.
Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.
Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.
"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."
Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.

He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.
The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.
He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.
A network of individuals working for the Russian intelligence services has operated since at least 2024, the US Justice Department said.
It said the so-called RIS Network had been conspiring and conducting attacks and murders on Russian dissidents and defectors around the world.

Five alleged members of the network had been accused of operating "as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin", Assistant Attorney General for national security John A Eisenberg said.
The five people alleged to be responsible for organising the plots are Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro.
All five remain at large, the Justice Department said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when the indictment was unsealed that he would not comment on the charges until he had heard or seen "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".

articles.title: North and South Korea trade accusations over landmines that injured three soldiers
articles.summary: A mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers has renewed scrutiny of North Korea's actions along the border and raised questions about its strategic goals.

image.caption: North Korea has been fortifying the border after a shift in policy against Seoul, calling it a 'foe' [FILE: June 2019]Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pyongyang and Seoul are trading increasingly hostile accusations across the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides the peninsula, 10 days after three South Korean soldiers were injured by a land mine on the South's side of the border.

The latest tensions may reflect a broader North Korean effort to test South Korea's resolve while extending its control to the outer limits of its territory, including an area that has effectively been a no-man's land for more than 70 years, according to a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University's department of Chinese studies
"The North revised its constitution in March this year and officially stated that they intend to define the absolute geographical limits of the nation, and that includes within the DMZ," said Choo.
"They want to maximize their territory and it is my sense that they would like to push the Military Demarcation Line [MDL] — the half-way point in the DMZ — further south," he told DW.
"I see the placing of landmines on the South's side of the line as a purely political act by the North, an attempt to threaten and intimidate the South."
Why Seoul blames North Korea

The three men were part of an 18-strong patrol clearing a new route through the DMZ as part of an investigation into the activities of North Korean troops in the western sector of the zone. The 4-kilometer-wide strip of land has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953.

blocks.caption: The DMZ is a fortified buffer zone between the two Koreas that has been in place since 1953Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Shortly before 11 a.m. on September 21, the patrol was around 10 meters south of the MDL when a staff sergeant detonated a mine. A second mine went off as the unit commander approached to provide assistance. Both men were successfully evacuated and have undergone surgery, with a third soldier treated for minor wounds.

The South Korean military has conducted an investigation with the United Nations Command, which administers the armistice on the border, and concluded in a report released this week that the mine was of North Korean origin.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday accused the North of sowing mines to the south of the MDL, a breach of the armistice agreement, and demanded an apology from Pyongyang and a commitment to halt the construction of further fortifications along the border.

"This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations, said in a press briefing.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, such as its so-called 'border fortification.' We strongly demand an apology and responsible measures from the North," Kang added.
In a statement, the UN Command said it had "determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred. UNC is addressing the violation through established Armistice mechanisms."
Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine
Many in the South are demanding more resolute action on the grounds that failure to respond will be taken as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

Na Kyung-won, a politician from the conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), has demanded that the South Korean military carry out exercises simulating a "decapitation attack" against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
She has also called for the restart of propaganda broadcasts from loudspeakers on the border and for dissident groups to be allowed to launch balloons carrying propaganda into the North.
A pattern of border confrontations

Yu Yong-weon, also of the PPP, told reporters on Wednesday that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL around 20 times in August and on 30 occasions in September. On each occasion, South Korean troops fired warning shots when the incursions were detected.

An editorial in the Korea JoongAng Daily on Thursday said North Korea must be "held accountable" for the incident, arguing that Pyongyang's denial of responsibility "demands a firm response, clear accountability and stronger border enforcement."

blocks.caption: Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong has accused Seoul of conspiracy after it blamed Pyongyang for the blast in the DMZImage: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The North is not backing down, however, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accusing the South of staging a provocation and threatening to retaliate.

In a statement published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong dismissed the South's allegations as a "self-staged farce" and accused the "South Korean armed gangs" of using the incident to justify political and military provocations against Pyongyang.
Accident or calculated provocation?
Andrei Lankov, a professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University, is more willing to view the landmine detonations as an accident.

"It makes no sense to me for North Korea to do this deliberately," he said. "At the moment, the North wants to keep a low profile and do nothing that could provoke the South. There is no gain in a deliberate attack like this."

Lankov believes a more likely scenario is that the mines were shifted from the northern side of the MDL in heavy rain or natural movements of the terrain, meaning that the North's protestations of innocence are genuine.

"I also do not think the South Korean government has any interest in escalating the situation further and that they will hope this is quickly forgotten," he said. "They will want to brush it under the carpet."
Choo, however, is less convinced and senses a growing anger in South Korean society that the government is not standing up to provocations from north of the border.

"I believe that resuming the propaganda broadcasts over the border would be an effective response, but I do not believe this government will do that," he said. "This government is trying very hard to connect with the North, but I see a failure to take a firm line this time being interpreted in the North as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

"Not responding would give Pyongyang a green light to push a little more and then a little more again," he said. "There is a lot of anger here that the government is not doing enough to protect soldiers who are serving on the DMZ, to protect the people and to protect our territory."
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs

articles.title: Zimbabwe tycoon Wicknell Chivayo dies in helicopter crash
articles.summary: Zimbabwe's President Emmerson Mnangagwa has confirmed the death of businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife in a helicopter crash, calling the high-rollers with a lavish lifestyle "consummately…

image.caption: Wicknell Chivayo was well known in Zimbabwe and had close ties to several African leadersImage: Instagram/sir_wicknell

blocks.text: The family of Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and President Emmerson Mnangagwa have confirmed reports that he and his wife Lucy Muteke were involved in a fatal helicopter crash southeast of Harare on Wednesday evening.
Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo told state broadcaster ZBC that the 43-year-old tycoon and his wife were killed in the crash, saying, "We are at a loss for words after the tragic news."
President Mnangagwa said the sudden and unexpected deaths "left our nation, my family, and me personally numbed and in deep shock and grief."
Chivayo was a prominent supporter of Mnangagwa who had secured a series of lucrative government contracts and was known for his lavish lifestyle and often-ostentatious gifts to allies and associates.
What do we know about the crash?
The helicopter crashed with six people on board in the rural Marondera district of Zimbabwe, not far southeast of Harare. There were no survivors.

Initially, as reports circulated that Chivayo was on board, a government spokesman said only that a "high-profile businessman" was one of four passengers. Police also said that they were conducting DNA tests and conducting other checks to confirm the identities of the victims, whose remains had been burned in a fire.
Mnangagwa published a tribute to Chivayo and his family the following day online.

"We are all shattered by this unexpected, sudden demise of so young a family," he wrote. "Consummately philanthropic, the Chivayo Family touches so many lives in our nation through its countless acts of charity and generosity which ran into millions of dollars, and which motivated and transformed countless lives."

"Tellingly, the Chivayos lost their lives on their way back from Gandami in rural Chikomba where they were putting up modern family and community structures, all in line with our policy on rural development through investments, industrialization, development and transformation," Mnangagwa wrote.
Who was Wicknell Chivayo?

Chivayo cultivated close ties both with Mnangagwa and the ruling ZANU-PF party, but also with other African leaders, including South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, Eswatini's King Mswati III, and Kenyan President William Ruto.

"Wicknell was a dear friend whose warmth touched many people. I will remember him for his friendship, his energy and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent," Ruto wrote in a tribute online.

Going by the handle "Sir Wicknell" in his social media persona, Chivayo would often post images of himself with Zimbabwean and African leaders. He was also known for a lavish lifestyle with luxury cars, designer clothing, and often for giving high-value gifts to associates, business partners, religious leaders, or even social media followers voicing support for him or for Mnangagwa.

Critics would often point to these close ties and to Chivayo as a case study of Zimbabwe's small elite class benefitting from large government contracts in a country with estimated median wages of less than US $5 per day.

Chivayo always denied allegations of corruption but faced several legal investigations that never resulted in convictions, starting with a 2005 money laundering case. He was arrested in 2018 in connection with the alleged misuse of a large advance payment tied to a solar power project, but five years later a judge dismissed the case, citing delays by prosecutors.

blocks.caption: President Mnangagwa lauded Chivayo, saying it was telling that he died on his return from a visit to an impoverished area where he was coordinating a development projectImage: Tsvangirayi Mukwazh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "His generous hand cut across sectors and reached many individuals: in politics, religion, public service, culture, sport and many different professions," Mnangagwa said of Chivayo.
"The late Wicknell Chivayo had a grand vision for his family, for our country, for the Southern African subregion and for our African continent."

articles.title: What it was like being in the room for Christa Pike's botched execution

image.caption: Media witnesses leave Riverbend Maximum Security Institution after the execution of Christa Pike was halted Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026, in Nashville, Tenn. (George Walker IV/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: As It Happens
Reporter Will Puckett says he may never sign up to witness another execution after what happened to Christa Pike, but he has no regrets about being there.
'This is not normal,' witness reporters said as Pike kept talking long after her lethal injection

Puckett, the morning co-anchor for WVLT-TV in Knoxville, Tenn., was one of seven journalists selected to bear witness to the execution of Christa Pike, who remains alive and in critical condition despite being administered two doses of pentobarbital on Wednesday.

"When you agree to be a state-selected witness to an event like this, you know there's the possibility that you'll be called upon to walk people through the events that could be traumatic," Puckett told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
"And that's exactly where we're at today, is just relaying how the state of Tennessee failed to execute Christa Gail Pike appropriately and properly."
LISTEN | Interview with media witness Will Puckett:
As It Happens6:52What it was like being in the room for Christa Pike's botched execution

Pike, 50, was 18 in January 1995 when she, her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, and a third companion lured their classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, into a wooded area where they tortured and killed her.

Pike and Shipp confessed to the killing and were convicted of first-degree murder. Pike was sentenced to death while Schipp, who was 17 at the time of the crime, was sentenced to life in prison. Years later, Pike expressed remorse for what she'd done.
Her lawyers and supporters tried to secure a stay of execution, citing her age at the time of the crime, mental health issues and a history of severe childhood neglect and sexual abuse.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, spoke out in favour of the execution, saying she has waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
'She should not be talking'
When Puckett and the other witnesses entered the execution chamber on Wednesday and took their seats at 6:41 p.m, a curtain and blinds covered the window, behind which Pike was strapped to a gurney.
He says that state witnesses are not shown the process of the needle being inserted into person's arm.
It was Puckett's first time attending an execution. He says the other reporters, who had been through it before, told him the whole process should take about 30 minutes.
But by the time a half-hour passed, officials hadn't yet opened the curtain.

"One of Christa Gail Pike's objections going into her execution is that she had small veins," Puckett said. "So if you listen to her complaint and go back to her medical history, you can only begin to connect the dots that they were having issues finding where her vein was to start the injection."
Death row inmate survives execution in Tennessee
When the curtains opened at 7:26, Pike seemed almost "jovial," Puckett said. She delivered her final words.
"She simply said, 'I'm going to leave this world the way that I've spent most of my life, in love,'" he said.

"She added at points, 'I'm going to love the people who hate on me the most because they're the ones who need the most love,' ending it with, 'I'm good now. I'm at peace. I'm ready to be free, I'm going to celebrate my freedom. This is a good day.'"
She did not mention Colleen Slemmer or her crime, he says.
Pike expressed physical discomfort, he said.
"She said, 'The vein in my arm feels like it's about to bust.' That was 7:33. One minute later, she goes, 'One spot is really throbbing,'" he said.

"That's when my colleagues, who have witnessed executions before, looked at me and said, 'This is not normal. She should not be talking. She should very clearly be in the process of dying.' And she wasn't."
'Why are we not viewing this?'
Pike took a few more deep breaths, then gasped, Puckett said. At 7:46 p.m., officials closed the curtains again for three minutes.
When the curtain re-opened, Pike was snoring. At about 8:05 p.m., officials closed the curtains again.
"There was a bunch [of people saying]: 'This obviously is not going right. What can you tell us? Why are we not viewing this?'" Puckett said.
The reporters did not get answers to their questions, and Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the curtain until the microphone was cut off at about 8:53 p.m.
Media witnesses were then escorted out.
Randall Spivey, one of Pike's lawyers, told reporters ⁠on Thursday afternoon that his client is a Nashville hospital receiving "life-saving medical care."
"Christa is alive right now," he said. "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment."
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee ordered a suspension of scheduled executions in Tennessee for the rest ⁠of the year and a third-party review of Wednesday's failed attempt.

items: What happened in Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike and what comes next?
Tennessee governor orders outside review after death row inmate Christa Pike survives execution attempt

blocks.text: Asked how he's feeling after Wednesday's ordeal, Puckett shifted focus away from himself.
"Our job's not to be the centre of attention, and I have tried my hardest to put myself into, for lack of a better term, robot mode," he said. "I'm OK right now."
In a case as high-profile and divisive as Pike's, Puckett says he takes seriously his "duty" to be "an unbiased witness" to what happened on Wednesday night.

"It definitely has me thinking on if I'll ever do this again," he said. "But it was an important thing to be able to say: I am in this room to make sure that the state does this properly, and be the eyes and ears of the general public who will not get to see anything that happens in this room."
With files from The Associated Press. Interview with Will Puckett produced by Chris Harbord

articles.title: What happened in failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.summary: The convicted killer is in hospital in Tennessee after surviving two lethal injections, in a case that has raised many questions.

blocks.text: What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in hospital and being given "life-saving measures" after Tennessee authorities failed in their attempt to execute her by lethal injection.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
What happened?
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was perpetrated alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.
She was scheduled to be put to death on Wednesday evening, local time. The injections were allowed by the US Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two syringes of the drug pentobarbital, though her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
The Tennessee Department of Correction defended the method it used, and said "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities have yet to provide their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike proved to be non-fatal, although medical experts have provided theories of their own.

Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure.
What happens next?
The state correction department added that Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility.
One of her lawyers said she was "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital.
Her health status is unclear as of Thursday morning.
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by the state governor, Bill Lee, who also says the year's last remaining execution will not go ahead as planned.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend

blocks.text: Image source, Family handout
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend
Opponents of the death penalty have similarly been quick to react.

Maya Foa, the chief executive of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain – lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. There is a historical precedent of authorities making a second attempt to execute those on death row.
Meanwhile Shipp, Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant, remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law. He was 17 at the time that Slemmer was killed.
What is the drug pentobarbital?

Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.

Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review - which took place under the presidency of Joe Biden - raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
His government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
The department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
Has this happened before?
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.

The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.

In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.
The DPI says lethal injection has the high­est rate of botched exe­cu­tions.

An incident in Oklahoma in 2014 gained particular notoriety. The execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because the lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured, and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.

In the US, 27 of the 50 states have the death penalty under state law. The federal government can also carry out executions after President Donald Trump, a supporter of capital punishment, ended a moratorium last year, However, it is yet to actually carry out any executions since then.

articles.title: British Sikh activist released from Delhi jail after nine-year detention
articles.summary:
Indian government issued with warning it would be in contempt of court if it failed to release Jagtar Singh Johal

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi…

blocks.text: The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.

Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.

The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.

On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings.

Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.

His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.

The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”

Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.

The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
In letters from the Delhi jail to the ministry seeking clarification on his release, the jail authorities said there were no further grounds for his detention.
They pointed out release warrants were issued on Monday after all the court’s bail conditions had been met, and any further detention without a court order amounted to administrative detention.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

articles.title: Kanye West's Russia shows officially cancelled after weeks of uncertainty
articles.summary: Chaos has surrounded the St Petersburg shows since the stadium said it had not agreed to host the rapper.

blocks.text: Russia was invaded by the Nazis in World War Two, and the country's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman was among those who criticised the planned shows.
Maria Zakharova said they were unacceptable and pointed out West's "glorification" of Hitler.
In 2025 West started selling swastika T-shirts and released a song called Heil Hitler.
Pro-war bloggers in Russia also questioned whether the country should be hosting an American artist while the US provided financial and military support for Ukraine.
West is yet to comment publicly on the cancellation.
His first major concert in the US for more than five years was held in Los Angeles in April, and he has since played in countries including Spain, Portugal and the Netherlands.
However, his Russian shows aren't the only gigs to have been cancelled.
Last summer West was set to headline London's Wireless Festival but was barred from entering the UK, forcing organisers to cancel the whole event.
West shows were also cancelled in Poland, Italy and France.

articles.title: Trump's AI rebrand causes 'unprecedented' demand for Slovenian website names
articles.summary: The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian domains.

blocks.text: President Donald Trump's push to rename AI may be behind an "unprecedented" rise in registrations for domain names in Slovenia, according to its official national registry.
The president wants AI to be called super intelligence - or SI - the same initials used by Slovenian websites.
Register.si spokesperson Klara Herman said 44,000 web addresses with the .si suffix had been registered in September, compared to less than 2,000 in August - an increase of more than 2,100%.
She said the scale of activity in late September was "unprecedented" compared to the previous 12 months.
President Trump called for the technology to be renamed during his speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on 11 September.
"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said.
"It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful... welcome to the new world of super intelligence."
Internet domains are the unique human-readable addresses people type into their web browsers to access websites - like bbc.co.uk.

Herman said registrations for .si web addresses in September stood out "very clearly" against the other months in the year, although she was "cautious" about attributing the entire increase to only President Trump's comments.
She said on 30 September alone, 11,000 new registrations were recorded.
One possible explanation for the purchases is cyber-squatting - where people speculatively register specific domain names in case they increase in value later on and can be sold for a profit.
For example, in 1997 Rick Schwartz, known as "The Domain King", bought the domain name men.com for $15,000 (£11,300). He sold it for $1.32 million seven years later.
On Tuesday, President Trump hosted a meeting of top technology bosses for what he called "an extraordinary gathering" of the people "building America's Golden Age".
He signed an executive order instructing US government departments and agencies to start using the terms "SI" and "Super Intelligence" and they should no longer acknowledge the use of the term AI.
SI will take the place of AI in "official correspondence", websites, reports and other forms of communication, the order said.
Images of the signatures for the order were mocked online, external however - when it was discovered "United States" had been spelt incorrectly underneath President Trump's signature.

articles.title: Explosions heard in Ethiopia's capital after drone flights banned
articles.summary: It comes a week after fighting erupted north of the capital between the army and a new alliance of armed groups.

blocks.text: Explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopia's capital, some in the area of the military headquarters in the west and another in the south of the city, residents and diplomatic sources say.

The blasts came hours after drone flights were banned over Addis Ababa and a week after fighting erupted in the north between the army and a newly launched alliance of armed groups including forces from the Tigray region.
A source linked to the opposition fighters told the Reuters news agency they were behind what they said were drone strikes.
"It was very loud. It was strong enough to set off car alarms," a resident in a southern area of the city, near the base of the secret service, told BBC Amharic.
He estimated that he heard the explosion in the Gotera neighbourhood some time around 00:30 local time (21:30 GMT).
Another resident told the BBC that he and his friends were playing games when they heard an explosion.
He lives in the western suburb of Torhayloch, a neighbourhood close to the military headquarters.
There were no official reports confirming the cause of the explosions, the exact locations affected or whether there were any casualties or damage.
The office of Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, the defence ministry as well as the federal and Addis Ababa police have not responded to BBC requests for comment.

articles.title: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could see drivers pay higher running costs while also increasing carbon emissions.
articles.summary: Weakened US fuel-efficiency rules and promises of cheaper cars could yet see drivers pay higher running costs while increasing planet-heating emissions.

image.caption: Gas prices are on the rise as Trump moves to make cars less fuel efficientImage: Mario Tama/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: As part of its "Freedom Means More Affordable Cars" initiative, the US Department of Transportation this week rolled back fuel efficiency rules under the guise of lowering vehicle prices.

The Trump administration's transport agency says US taxpayers will save $138 billion (€122 billion) over the next five years — new vehicles will be $1,300 cheaper on average — since automakers will no longer have to invest in more fuel-efficient fleets.
But this does not account for soaring gas prices as Middle East conflicts choke global supply.

"Any savings on the front end get eaten up and spat out by excess costs of fuel … Fuel economy standards have saved drivers hundreds of billions of dollars," said Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse in a social media post.

Under the revised Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) rules, vehicle fleets only require an average fuel efficiency of about 35 miles per gallon (14.7km per liter) by 2031, down around one-third from 50 miles per gallon.

Implemented by the Biden administration in 2024, the updated efficiency rules aimed to incentivize the production of low emission electric vehicles and hybrids. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) estimates the standards would have saved 70 billion gallons (265 billion litres) of fuel over 25 years.

blocks.caption: Drivers in the US will be pumping more gas under weakened fuel efficiency rules Image: Brandon Bell/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: Meanwhile, nonprofit advocacy group, the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) says an earlier version of CAFE regulations has saved US consumers have saved about $321 billion at the gas pump since 2010.
Rollbacks set to increase planet-heating emissions

The world's biggest petrol consumer, the US burns through 20 million barrels of oil per day, which is 20% of global consumption, notes Dan Becker, director of the Safe Climate Transport Campaign at the US-based nonprofit environmental group Center for Biological Diversity.
"Transportation is the biggest consumer of that oil, making strong auto standards the most effective way to cut pollution and oil use," Becker said in a statement.

The rules that have been diluted this week would have prevented more than 710 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions by 2050 — the equivalent of running 165 million gas-powered passenger vehicles for a year.

"With transportation representing nearly 28% of US greenhouse emissions, rolling back fuel economy standards is a dangerous setback for near-term climate goals," said Ben Scott, head of Energy Demand at UK-based climate think tank, Carbon Tracker.
"It risks keeping inefficient combustion engines on the road much longer than climate science demands," he told DW.

But following the Trump administration’s elimination of greenhouse gas emissions standards for light- and heavy-duty vehicles last year, Dave Cooke, senior vehicles analyst for the UCS Clean Transportation Program, said the rollbacks merely compound "a much more significant step backwards."
He said the trend sends "a specific signal to automakers," adding that "the United States is seeking to maximize oil usage to increase oil company profits."
This will be to the detriment of climate targets, with high-polluting oil contributing one-third of global fossil fuel emissions that continue to rise — along with temperatures.
The world just had the hottest August on record as severe heatwaves in Europe caused over 16,000 excess deaths in Germany alone.
US turns its back on EVs
Can US transport still transition to clean energy?
Sales of low emission EVs are down in the US in 2026, especially after president Trump scrapped the $7,500 tax credit for new electric vehicles.
American automakers also continue to push back against regulations that would incentivize a switch to EVs, arguing there is a lack of consumer demand.

"It's highly unlikely that the United States will suddenly become awash in electric options when neither the auto industry nor regulators seem interested in providing such choices for consumers," said Cooke.
But Ben Scott believes that while softening US fuel economy standards "will create temporary headwinds", it won't stall an inevitable transition to electric vehicles.

"With EVs delivering vastly lower running costs, electrification becomes a clear-cut economic choice," he said of cars running on "cheaper, domestically secure energy that will drive the transition forward, regardless of short-term politics."
As less efficient cars and trucks consume more oil that's more expensive and in shorter supply, "the fragility of oil-dependent transport" is set to be exposed, he said.

articles.title: Tennessee governor halts executions after second botched lethal injection attempt this year – US politics live
articles.summary: Bill Lee pauses state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year after inmate Christa Pike survives two lethal injections

blocks.text: Tennessee governor halts executions after second botched lethal injection attempt this year
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Tennessee governor Bill Lee has halted the state’s remaining executions for the rest of the year after officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death yesterday.

Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn’t been told about her condition.
She had been scheduled for execution at 10am on Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.
Governor Lee said that he was halting the one remaining execution for the rest of 2026 and ordered a “comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.”

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” Lee said in a statement.
The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that they “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”

Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. The state’s execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution. In May, state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.

blocks.text: Trump officials abandon effort to investigate election threats, experts warn

blocks.caption: George Chidi

blocks.text: George Chidi

The Trump administration has abandoned key security bodies meant to investigate direct threats to US elections by foreign actors and domestic terrorists, according to former officials and a recent report.

While administration officials have been actively focused on unsubstantiated claims of widespread voter fraud by noncitizens, other credible election threats appear to have been overlooked, the officials say.

Between 2021 and 2024, the justice department’s election threats taskforce prosecuted 21 cases, like that of Solomon Peña, a failed candidate for the New Mexico house of representatives who organized shootings at the houses of election officials, or Quintez Brown, who shot up a campaign meeting of Louisville’s mayor.

Democrats and Republicans faced prosecution for harassing, intimidating and threatening elections workers, noted Nikki Fisher, former chief election security officer for the Oregon secretary of state, now the executive director of the Oregon District Attorneys Association.
Since then, the taskforce seems to have gone quiet.

“While officials are being trained to handle threats, the federal deterrent meant to punish the people making them appears to have gone quiet,” Fisher said. “To date, no new cases have been prosecuted, and the DoJ’s election threats taskforce appears to be defunct in practice.”

articles.title: Germans' biggest fear is the high cost of living, an annual study finds
articles.summary: What do Germans fear most in 2026? Wars? Global crises? Wrong. Their biggest concern is the cost of living, which keeps rising.

image.caption: Germans see the price of groceries, energy risingImage: Frank Hoermann/SvenSimon/picture alliance

blocks.text: People in Germany are more politically engaged than they have been in a long time. This was also evident in the high voter turnout in the September state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
Germans are passionately debating immigration, the upcoming reforms to pensions, healthcare and long-term care, as well as democracy and the rule of law.

But by far their greatest fear is the cost of living in Germany, which is becoming increasingly expensive. At least, that is the finding of the 2026 study on "Germans' Fears," which the insurer R+V presented in Berlin.
From early May through late July of this year, researchers surveyed some 2,400 German-speaking citizens aged 14 and older.
The cost of living is again their top concern, as it has been in the survey for many years in a row. This study has been conducted annually since the early 1990s.
Last year, 52% of those polled cited the rising cost of daily life as their greatest concern; in 2026, that figure has risen to 59%.
At a press conference in Berlin, Isabelle Borucki, a political scientist from Marburg who served as a consultant on the study, explained why.
"The price of key items — energy, housing and food — has risen noticeably. This reduces the financial leeway for leisure, vacations and purchases. People can afford less and less."
Germans worry about higher taxes and contributions
The study also shows that people are well aware that Germany's social security systems are in a serious crisis. Both the state pension fund and long-term care insurance are chronically in the red.
Most people also seem to realize that taxes and contributions will rise. That is why the fear of higher taxes is stronger than in previous years.

"Behind the fear of higher taxes and benefit cuts lies the question of fairness, with people wondering who will bear the costs of modernization," Borucki said. "And they worry, 'Can I still rely on getting benefits I am entitled to?'"
Less fear of war, immigration and Donald Trump
But what about the issues that are also dominating the headlines in Germany? What about immigration and the increasing polarization of society? Or global upheavals?
A narrow majority of 52% of those surveyed fear that the number of refugees is overwhelming the German state. This fear ranks third among all concerns.
But when it comes to global upheavals, Germans are not so concerned.
Only 45% of respondents fear that US President Donald Trump's policies are making the world a more dangerous place, researcher Grischa Brower-Rabinowitsch said.
"That's significantly fewer than during his first term."

In 2018, during Trump's first term, 69% responded to the same question by saying that this made them very afraid. "After years of constant geopolitical alarm bells, people are starting to get used to it," Brower-Rabinowitsch said.
Berlin has space, so why is housing so expensive?
German politicians got poor grades

This trend also seems to hold true for other areas of concern: Germans are looking to the future with considerably less anxiety than expected. Only 34% now fear a war involving Germany, down from 41% last year.

Since 1992, the study has asked people if they are afraid of losing their job? Currently, only 20% of the surveyed members of the working population answered "yes." That is the lowest figure ever recorded.

However, the assessment of politicians — both those in the government and those in the opposition — is sobering: Respondents were asked to grade politicians with one being the best and six the worst (the grading system used at German schools). The result was an average score of 4.1, which is barely a passing mark.

Political scientist Borucki places the primary responsibility on the current government of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) under Chancellor Friedrich Merz which came to power in May 2025.
After the end of the previous coalition government, many associated the new coalition with hopes for more leadership, less conflict and a rapid economic turnaround.
"That has not come to pass," says Borucki. "There is now a gap between the grand announcements and tangible results. People are disappointed and losing confidence."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: ‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of Trump
articles.summary:
Diehard Hugo Chávez supporters struggle to comprehend ideological U-turn being executed by Delcy Rodríguez’s interim administration

He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo…
articles.byline: Camille Rodríguez Montilla in Caracas and Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: He was one of the most passionate propagandists for Hugo Chávez’s Bolivarian revolution: a feisty leftist TV personality who spent more than two decades singing the movement’s praises on his state-funded show, The Razorblade.
Mario Silva’s devotion was such that he often hosted his programme with Chávez’s portrait behind him and he had El Comandante’s curly signature tattooed on to his left wrist.

But nine months after Venezuela’s political landscape was scrambled by Donald Trump’s abduction of Chávez’s heir, Nicolás Maduro, Silva’s show has been cancelled, and its host is livid about the revolution’s direction under Maduro’s former deputy, Delcy Rodríguez.

“[I feel] a lot of disappointment – depressed … and sometimes I wake up and feel like the world is collapsing around me,” the 66-year-old said during a rare interview at his home studio in the mountains outside the capital, Caracas.

Silva has spent recent weeks railing against Rodríguez’s interim administration on YouTube, his home since his programme on state TV was axed, berating those he blames for Venezuela’s “shameful and utterly illegitimate surrender” to the US.

Since January, a parade of high-ranking US officials – including the head of the CIA, the chair of the joint chiefs of staff and the energy secretary, Chris Wright – have visited Caracas, while Trump recently trumpeted striking “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Rodríguez’s regime. Last week, Rodríguez and Trump met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, posing for a smiley photograph that left diehard Chavistas such as Silva aghast.

“I thought it [the photo] was artificial intelligence or something like that. But it’s surrealism, utter surrealism … It’s impossible to understand,” Silva fumed on YouTube as a red flag emblazoned with the faces of Karl Marx, Friedrich Engels and Vladimir Lenin hung behind him.

blocks.caption: Mario Silva in his home studio in La Guaira state, Venezuela. Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian

blocks.text: “They have surrendered this country and surrendered it the most vile and despicable way,” Silva went on. “Honestly, they are dragging the country’s name through the mud. They are dragging Chávez’s name through the mud.”

In another broadcast, Silva seethed about the cosy post-Maduro relationship that has developed between one-time anti-imperialist flagbearers in Caracas and Trump officials: “Traitors and lackeys, you will have to answer for this!”

Silva is not the only Chavista loyalist struggling to comprehend the ideological U-turn being executed by Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president but has engineered a historic rapprochement with the US since his rendition on 3 January.

Elías Jaua, a vice-president and foreign minister under Chávez, is also up in arms, and claims the feeling is widely shared. “What I hear from comrades across the country is bewilderment, disagreement and indignation,” said Jaua, who believes Trump’s oil deal “amounts to an act of pillage against an entire nation”.

blocks.caption: Venezuela’s interior minister Diosdado Cabello addressing a crowd during a march in support of Delcy Rodríguez last week. Photograph: Diko Betancourt/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Juan Barreto, a former member of the ruling Socialist party (PSUV) and mayor of Caracas, said such an agreement would have been unimaginable when the Bolivarian revolution began after Chávez’s 1998 election. He said Chavistas, who had once vowed “Not a drop of oil to the empire if Venezuela is attacked!”, were now in effect saying: “All of the oil reserves [for the US], for as long as you want!”
“The current situation is one of tutelage,” Barreto said.

Rodríguez has defended the deal, claiming it will create more than $209bn (£158bn) in revenues that will help improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said in a recent TV broadcast.

Héctor Rodríguez, another prominent Chavista politician, has sought to deflect criticism of Venezuela’s interim government by recalling how Chávez was forced to make a tactical retreat after his failed coup attempt in 1992. “No one can tell me Chávez was a coward. He understood that the balance of power had shifted … and decided to take a step backwards,” Rodríguez said recently.

​Last week as Delcy Rodríguez met Trump in New York, thousands of people ​joined a pro-government rall​y in Caracas, where supporters parroted the slogan “Delcy avanza, tú tienes mi confianza!” (“Move forward, Delcy. I trust in you!”).

blocks.caption: Ex National Assembly deputy and television presenter Mario Silva in his home studio. Photograph: Andrea Hernández Briceño/The Guardian

blocks.text: “No matter how much they kick and scream, there’s nothing they can do to try to cover up the success of President Delcy Rodríguez’s visit to New York,” her interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, ​told the crowd. Unlike at previous marches, there was scant mention of Maduro and few calls for him to be released.
The depth and potential consequences of Chavista anger over Rodríguez’s embrace of Venezuela’s longtime foes in Washington remain unclear.

Orlando Pérez, a Latin America expert from the University of North Texas at Dallas, recognised there was indignation at what some considered a sellout of their anti-imperialist ideals. “There are Chavistas that are pissed off, there’s no question about it,” he said. “There are Chavistas who see this as a betrayal of Hugo Chávez and the betrayal of the movement.”

But Pérez believed that for many Chavistas who had remained in power after Trump’s invasion, the “pragmatic reality” was that working with Washington was “a necessary evil” if it meant keeping Venezuela’s opposition out of power.

“If that means negotiating with Trump, if that means dealing with the CIA etc, it’s fine,” he said. “Beyond whatever ideological position they might have … I suspect most of them are gritting their teeth and just going along with this process as long as they can stay in power and keep their jobs. I think for most it’s as simple as that: it’s about their material wellbeing.”

However, Pérez believed Rodríguez’s government would need to demonstrate to supporters “tangible benefits to the cooperation” with the US in order to avoid a backlash. “They’re going to have to show that these things have a material consequence to the lives of their social base … if you don’t deliver, then it is going to get very volatile,” he warned.

blocks.caption: A Venezuelan government supporter carries dolls depicting Hugo Chávez and the pro-government comic-book characters Super Bigote and Cilita at a march in Caracas backing Delcy Rodríguez’s participation in the UN general assembly in New York. Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: So far there has been no sign of significant resistance from outraged supporters of Chavismo. But Silva claimed the government’s new direction and economic policies could eventually trigger a social uprising and protests.

“Worsening economic conditions will degrade [people’s] quality of life, and that pressure is bound to explode. It has to explode – it’s not just wishful thinking. This isn’t a prediction born of desire, it’s an inevitability,” said the broadcaster, who has claimed he is facing investigation for alleged acts of “aggravated defamation and slander against the interim government”.

Silva lit one cigarette after another as he recalled the early hours of 3 January 2026 when, as US troops swept into Venezuela’s capital, he realised the revolution he had spent more than 20 years defending was not going to defend itself.

The Chavista broadcaster said he moved from one strategic point to another across Caracas before finally calling the commander at his assigned post. “I said: ‘Hey, what happened? Where are the weapons?’” Silva recalled, his face settling into a sad grin as he remembered the answer. “Go to sleep, Mario,” he was told.
Silva pauses. “You have no idea how disappointed I was.”

articles.title: Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
articles.summary: Capt Smit Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard the Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv.
articles.byline: Henry Moore, Sharanya Hrishikesh & Meryl Sebastian

blocks.text: Capt Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later. He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022, having become an experienced pilot.
Speaking to the BBC, Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, said he remembers Capt Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis.
"We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."
Capt Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".
Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.

Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.

Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.
"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.
He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.
"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.

At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.
He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."
Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.
The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.

Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.
At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.

He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.
The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.
"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.
Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".
Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.
"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

articles.title: Germany news: Merz lauds NATO with Westphalian Peace Prize
articles.summary: At a ceremony to honor NATO, the German chancellor warned that Russia will threaten the rest of Europe if it isn't stopped in Ukraine. In other news, the German military will set up its first drone…

image.caption: NATO chief Mark Rutte was present in Münster to receive the Westphalian Peace PrizeImage: Fabian Strauch/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 1, 2026
Merz warns: If Germany falters, Ukraine will too

blocks.caption: Before the award ceremony, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte visited the German-Dutch Corps in MünsterImage: Sem van der Wal/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a keynote speech on foreign policy, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz issued a stark warning against reducing aid to Ukraine in its defense against Russia.
"If we waver in Germany, then Europe wavers. If Europe wavers, then Ukraine wavers as well," he cautioned at the ceremony in Münster where the Westphalian Peace Prize was awarded to NATO.

Merz specifically warned that Russia could attack Germany and NATO if Ukraine falls. "If we fail to stop Moscow, then sooner or later, the Russian war machine will turn against us, against NATO itself. We must not turn a blind eye to this danger," he stressed.

The German chancellor emphasized that without German aid, the war against Ukraine would result in an "imposed peace." This would lead to mass migration toward the West and the destabilization of the Ukrainian state, according to Merz.
He touched only briefly on the meeting between Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in New York last weekend.

Merz said it was yet another example of how diplomatic efforts fell on deaf ears in Moscow. Russia understands only the “language of strength” and must be brought to the negotiating table through this approach, he stressed.

Merz said "unity and strength remain prerequisites for successful negotiations with Moscow. And this can only encourage us to keep the United States of America by our side in our policy regarding Ukraine".
Merz calls for unity against AfD

Merz said that a united front is also needed in Germany, where the far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) has seen significant success in recent state elections and currently leads in nationwide polls.

"We in Germany, too, will not allow ourselves to be divided," Merz said. "Not by hybrid attacks, not by social media agitation driven by Moscow-controlled bots, and... not by the slogans of the AfD and its Russian backers."
The AfD wants Berlin to stop providing military and financial support to Ukraine, lift sanctions against Russia, and restore dialogue.
What is Westphalian Peace Prize?
The Westphalian Peace Prize is awarded every two years by the Economic Society for Westphalia and Lippe (WWL).
The award commemorates the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, which was concluded in the town halls of Münster and Osnabrück.
It brought an end to the Thirty Years’ War and is regarded as a contribution to the European peace order among states with equal rights.
This year, NATO was honored for its contribution to the European peace order.

articles.title: K-pop star convicted of violating military service law
articles.summary: The member of K-pop band Winner was given a suspended prison sentence for repeated absences from his national service work.

blocks.text: A South Korean court has handed a suspended one-year prison sentence to K-pop singer Song Min-ho after he was convicted of violating the country's military service law.
The 33-year-old member of the boy band Winner was found to have been absent multiple times at a community centre in Seoul, where he had worked as a social worker from 2023 to 2024.
All able-bodied men in South Korea have to serve at least 18 months in the military. But some are alternatively assigned as social service personnel for health reasons.
The prison sentence handed on Thursday is suspended for two years. That means he can avoid incarceration if he does not commit any crime during that two-year probationary period.
The court heard that Song, who is also known by his stage name Mino, had recorded 102 unauthorised absences during his 21-month stint as a social service agent.
Military service is a duty to be performed "faithfully", and social service agents are "no exception", the court said.
But the court also noted that Song had admitted to the charges and shown remorse.

Authorities launched an investigation into Song shortly after he was discharged in 2024, when local media reported that he was frequently absent from his social service duties and took excessive sick leave.
Song's supervisor at the social service centre was also given a suspended jail sentence for helping him dodge his duties, including falsifying records to make it look like Song had reported to work.
The conscription of South Korea's entertainers has long been a topic of national public debate.

Gangnam Style singer Psy famously had to enlist twice, once in 2003 and another time in 2007, after a Seoul court ruled that he had neglected his duties by continuing his showbiz activities during his first national service stint.

Steve Yoo, one of the country's biggest pop stars in the 1990s and early 2000s, was embroiled in a national scandal after he was found to have evaded military service in 2002. South Korean authorities banned him from the country after he renounced his citizenship and became a US national shortly before he was due to serve in the military.

Going on hiatus to serve in the military is often a threat for budding careers in South Korea's fast-moving entertainment industry. But the evasion of military service also comes with intense public scrutiny and legal repercussions.
Ahead of the ruling on Thursday, Song told reporters that he regretted his actions and was "sorry toward the people who gave me so much love", Seoul Economic Daily reported.
But he did not answer a question about whether he would re-enlist to serve the mandatory duty.

articles.title: Netanyahu says too early to tell who was behind plane incident as flydubai halts all flights to Israel
articles.summary:
Israeli prime minister cautions against early conclusions when asked if there were any signs of Iranian involvement

Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately…

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the apparent attempt to crash a ⁠Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight, even as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations called the incident a “terror attack”, without apportioning blame.

Danny Danon told Fox News on Wednesday night that Israel had “no doubt that it was a terror attack from a radical individual. We still cannot link it to a terror state or terror organisation, but for sure we know there was an intention to bring that plane down.”
Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation takes place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.

The incident – which began when one pilot stabbed another on the flight deck in an apparent attempt to take control of the aircraft – is under investigation. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had more than 170 people on board, most of them from Israel.

In what have been hailed as acts of tremendous bravery, several passenger rushed the cockpit of the flight and wrestled the controls from the alleged attacker even as the plane descended sharply, managing to eventually taking control and stabilising the plane before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
